entries.3733822dac663c4b220ab591b10c00e5b4bc3fdb: <div sID="gen23276" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="22" osisID="Matt.22" sID="Matt.22"/> <div eID="gen23276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23277" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23278" type="x-p"/> This chapter is a continuation of Christ's discourses in the temple, two or three days before he died. His discourses then are largely recorded, as being of special weight and consequence. In this chapter, we have, I. Instruction given, by the parable of the marriage-supper, concerning the rejection of the Jews, and the calling of the Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.1-Matt.22.10">ver. 1-10</reference>), and, by the doom of the guest that had not the wedding-garment, the danger of hypocrisy in the profession of Christianity, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.11-Matt.22.14">ver. 11-14</reference>. II. Disputes with the Pharisees, Sadducees, and scribes, who opposed Christ, 1. Concerning paying tribute to Cæsar, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.15-Matt.22.22">ver. 15-22</reference>. 2. Concerning the resurrection of the dead, and the future state, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.23-Matt.22.33">ver. 23-33</reference>. 3. Concerning the great commandment of the law, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.34-Matt.22.40">ver. 34-40</reference>. 4. Concerning the relation of the Messiah to David, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.41-Matt.22.46">ver. 41-46</reference>.
entries.d9ac83c2205f81f56cffac9e9bfa9fd3ebca18a7: <div eID="gen23278" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23277" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Parable of the Marriage Feast.</title> <div sID="gen23279" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And Jesus answered and spake unto them again by parables, and said, <hi type="super">2</hi> The kingdom of heaven is like unto a certain king, which made a marriage for his son, <hi type="super">3</hi> And sent forth his servants to call them that were bidden to the wedding: and they would not come. <hi type="super">4</hi> Again, he sent forth other servants, saying, Tell them which are bidden, Behold, I have prepared my dinner: my oxen and <hi type="italic">my</hi> fatlings <hi type="italic">are</hi> killed, and all things <hi type="italic">are</hi> ready: come unto the marriage. 5 But they made light of <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and went their ways, one to his farm, another to his merchandise: <hi type="super">6</hi> And the remnant took his servants, and entreated <hi type="italic">them</hi> spitefully, and slew <hi type="italic">them.</hi> <hi type="super">7</hi> But when the king heard <hi type="italic">thereof,</hi> he was wroth: and he sent forth his armies, and destroyed those murderers, and burned up their city. <hi type="super">8</hi> Then saith he to his servants, The wedding is ready, but they which were bidden were not worthy. <hi type="super">9</hi> Go ye therefore into the highways, and as many as ye shall find, bid to the marriage. <hi type="super">10</hi> So those servants went out into the highways, and gathered together all as many as they found, both bad and good: and the wedding was furnished with guests. <hi type="super">11</hi> And when the king came in to see the guests, he saw there a man which had not on a wedding garment: <hi type="super">12</hi> And he saith unto him, Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment? And he was speechless. <hi type="super">13</hi> Then said the king to the servants, Bind him hand and foot, and take him away, and cast <hi type="italic">him</hi> into outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth. <hi type="super">14</hi> For many are called, but few <hi type="italic">are</hi> chosen. <div eID="gen23279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23280" type="x-p"/> We have here the parable of the guests invited to <hi type="italic">the wedding-feast.</hi> In this it is said (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.1">v. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">Jesus answered,</hi> not to what his opposers <hi type="italic">said</hi> (for they were put to silence), but to what they <hi type="italic">thought,</hi> when they were wishing for an opportunity to <hi type="italic">lay hands on him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.21.46">ch. xxi. 46</reference>. Note, Christ knows how to answer men's thoughts, for he is a Discerner of them. Or, He <hi type="italic">answered,</hi> that is, he continued his discourse to the same purport; for this parable represents the gospel offer, and the entertainment it meets with, as the former, but under another similitude. The parable of the vineyard represents the sin of the rulers that persecuted the prophets; it shows also the sin of the people, who generally neglected the message, while their great ones were persecuting the messengers. <div eID="gen23280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23281" type="x-p"/> I. Gospel preparations are here represented by a feast which a king made <hi type="italic">at the marriage of his son;</hi> such is <hi type="italic">the kingdom of heaven,</hi> such the provision made for precious souls, in and by the new covenant. The <hi type="italic">King</hi> is God, <hi type="italic">a great King, King of kings.</hi> Now, <div eID="gen23281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23282" type="x-p"/> 1. Here is <hi type="italic">a marriage made for his son,</hi> Christ is the Bridegroom, the church is the bride; the gospel-day is <hi type="italic">the day of his espousals,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.3.11">Cant. iii. 11</reference>. Behold by faith <hi type="italic">the church of the first-born, that are written in heaven,</hi> and were given to Christ by him whose they were; and in them you see <hi type="italic">the bride, the Lamb's wife,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.21.9">Rev. xxi. 9</reference>. The gospel covenant is a marriage covenant betwixt Christ and believers, and it is a marriage of God's making. This branch of the similitude is only mentioned, and not prosecuted here. <div eID="gen23282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23283" type="x-p"/> 2. Here is <hi type="italic">a dinner prepared for this marriage,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.22.4">v. 4</reference>. All the privileges of church-membership, and all the blessings of the new covenant, pardon of sin, the favour of God, peace of conscience, the promises of the gospel, and all the riches contained in them, access to the throne of grace, the comforts of the Spirit, and a well-grounded hope of eternal life. These are the preparations for this feast, a heaven upon earth now, and a heaven in heaven shortly. God has prepared it in his counsel, in his covenant. It is a dinner, denoting present privileges in the midst of our day, beside the supper at night in glory. <div eID="gen23283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23284" type="x-p"/> (1.) It is <hi type="italic">a feast.</hi> Gospel preparations were prophesied of as <hi type="italic">a feast</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.25.6">Isa. xxv. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">a feast of fat things,</hi> and were typified by the many festivals of the ceremonial law (<reference osisRef="1Cor.5.8">1 Cor. v. 8</reference>); <hi type="italic">Let us keep the feast.</hi> A <hi type="italic">feast is a good day</hi> (<reference osisRef="Esth.7.17">Esth. vii. 17</reference>); so is the gospel; it is a continual feast. <hi type="italic">Oxen and fatlings are killed</hi> for this feast; no niceties, but substantial food; enough, and enough of the best. The day of a feast is <hi type="italic">a day of slaughter,</hi> or sacrifice, <reference osisRef="Jas.5.5">Jam. v. 5</reference>. Gospel preparations are all founded in the death of Christ, his sacrifice of himself. A feast was made for love, it is a reconciliation feast, a token of God's goodwill toward men. It was made <hi type="italic">for laughter</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.19">Eccl. x. 19</reference>), it is a rejoicing feast. It was made for fulness; the design of the gospel was to fill every <hi type="italic">hungry soul with good things.</hi> It was made for fellowship, to maintain an intercourse between heaven and earth. We are sent for <hi type="italic">to the banquet of wine, that we may tell what is our petition, and what is our request.</hi> <div eID="gen23284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23285" type="x-p"/> (2.) It is a <hi type="italic">wedding feast.</hi> Wedding feasts are usually rich, free, and joyful. The first miracle Christ wrought, was, to make plentiful provision for a wedding feast (<reference osisRef="John.2.7">John ii. 7</reference>); and surely then he will not be wanting in provision for his own wedding feast, when <hi type="italic">the marriage of the Lamb is come, and the bride hath made herself ready,</hi> a victorious triumphant feast, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.7">Rev. xix. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.17">17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.18">18</reference>. <div eID="gen23285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23286" type="x-p"/> (3.) It is a <hi type="italic">royal wedding feast;</hi> it is <hi type="italic">the feast of a king</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.36">1 Sam. xxv. 36</reference>), at the marriage, not of a servant, but of a son; and then, if ever, he will, like Ahasuerus, show <hi type="italic">the riches of his glorious kingdom,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.1.4">Esth. i. 4</reference>. The provision made for believers in the covenant of grace, is not such as worthless worms, like us, had any reason to expect, but such as it becomes <hi type="italic">the King of glory</hi> to give. He gives like himself; for he gives himself to be to them <hi type="italic">El shaddai—a God that is enough,</hi> a feast indeed for a soul. <div eID="gen23286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23287" type="x-p"/> II. Gospel calls and offers are represented by an invitation to this feast. Those that make a feast will have guests to grace the feast with. God's guests are the children of men. <hi type="italic">Lord, what is man,</hi> that he should be thus dignified! <hi type="italic">The guests</hi> that were first invited were the Jews; wherever the gospel is preached, this invitation is given; ministers are the <hi type="italic">servants</hi> that are sent to invite, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.4-Prov.9.5">Prov. ix. 4, 5</reference>. <div eID="gen23287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23288" type="x-p"/> Now, 1. The guests <hi type="italic">are called, bidden</hi> to the wedding. All that are within hearing of the joyful sound of the gospel, to them is the word of this invitation sent. The servants that bring the invitation do not set down their names in a paper; there is no occasion for that, since none are excluded but those that exclude themselves. <hi type="italic">Those that are bidden to the dinner are bidden to the wedding;</hi> for all that partake of gospel privileges are to give a due and respectful attendance on the Lord Jesus, as the faithful friends and humble servants of the Bridegroom. They are <hi type="italic">bidden to the wedding,</hi> that they may <hi type="italic">go forth to meet the bridegroom;</hi> for it is the Father's will that <hi type="italic">all men should honour the Son.</hi> <div eID="gen23288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23289" type="x-p"/> 2. The guests are called upon; for in the gospel there are not only gracious proposals made, but gracious persuasives. <hi type="italic">We persuade men, we beseech them in Christ's stead,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.11">2 Cor. v. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.20">20</reference>. See how much Christ's heart is set upon the happiness of poor souls! He not only provides for them, in consideration of their want, but sends to them, in consideration of their weakness and forgetfulness. When the invited guests were slack in coming, the king <hi type="italic">sent forth other servants,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.22.4">v. 4</reference>. When the prophets of the Old Testament prevailed not, nor John the Baptist, nor Christ himself, who told them the entertainment was almost ready (<hi type="italic">the kingdom of God was at hand</hi>), the apostles and ministers of the gospel were sent after Christ's resurrection, to tell them it was come, it was quite ready; and to persuade them to accept the offer. One would think it had been enough to give men an intimation that they had leave to come, and should be welcome; that, during the solemnity of the wedding, the king kept open house; but, because <hi type="italic">the natural man discerns not,</hi> and therefore desires not, <hi type="italic">the things of the Spirit of God,</hi> we are pressed to accept the call by the most powerful inducements, <hi type="italic">drawn with the cords of a man, and all the bonds of love.</hi> If the repetition of the call will move us, <hi type="italic">Behold, the Spirit saith, Come; and the bride saith, Come; let him that heareth say, Come; let him that is athirst come,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.22.17">Rev. xxii. 17</reference>. If the reason of the call will work upon us, <hi type="italic">Behold, the dinner is prepared, the oxen and fatlings are killed, and all things are ready;</hi> the Father is ready to accept of us, the Son to intercede for us, the Spirit to sanctify us; pardon is ready; peace is ready, comfort is ready; the promises are ready, as <hi type="italic">wells of living water</hi> for supply; ordinances are ready, as golden pipes for conveyance; angels are ready to attend us, creatures are ready to be in league with us, providences are ready to work for our good, and heaven, at last, is ready to receive us; it is <hi type="italic">a kingdom prepared, ready to be revealed in the last time.</hi> Is all this ready; and shall we be unready? Is all this preparation made for us; and is there any room to doubt of our welcome, if we come in a right manner? Come, therefore, O <hi type="italic">come to the marriage; we beseech you, receive not</hi> all this <hi type="italic">grace of God in vain,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.1">2 Cor. vi. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen23289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23290" type="x-p"/> III. The cold treatment which the gospel of Christ often meets with among the children of men, represented by the cold treatment that this message met with and the hot treatment that the messengers met with, in both which the king himself and the royal bridegroom are affronted. This reflects primarily upon the Jews, who rejected the counsel of God against themselves; but it looks further, to the contempt that would, by many in all ages, be put upon, and the opposition that would be given to, the gospel of Christ. <div eID="gen23290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23291" type="x-p"/> 1. The message was basely slighted (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.3">v. 3</reference>); <hi type="italic">They would not come.</hi> Note, The reason why sinners come not to Christ and salvation by him is, not because they <hi type="italic">cannot,</hi> but because <hi type="italic">they will not</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.5.40">John v. 40</reference>); <hi type="italic">Ye will not come to me.</hi> This will aggravate the misery of sinners, that they might have had happiness for the coming for, but it was their own act and deed to refuse it. <hi type="italic">I would, and ye would not.</hi> But this was not all (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.5">v. 5</reference>); <hi type="italic">they made light of it;</hi> they thought it not worth coming for; thought the messengers made more ado than needs; let them magnify the preparations ever so much, they could feast as well at home. Note, Making light of Christ, and of the great salvation wrought out by him, is the damning sin of the world. <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Amelesantes</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">They were careless.</hi> Note, Multitudes perish eternally through mere carelessness, who have not any direct aversion, but a prevailing indifference, to the matters of their souls, and an unconcernedness about them. <div eID="gen23291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23292" type="x-p"/> And the reason why <hi type="italic">they made light of the marriage feast</hi> was, because they had other things that they minded more, and had more mind to; <hi type="italic">they went their ways, one to his farm, and another to his merchandise.</hi> Note, The business and profit of worldly employments prove to many a great hindrance in closing with Christ: none turn their back on the feast, but with some plausible excuse or other, <reference osisRef="Luke.14.18">Luke xiv. 18</reference>. The country people have their farms to look after, about which there is always something or other to do; the town's people must tend their shops, and be constant upon the exchange; they must <hi type="italic">buy, and sell, and get gain.</hi> It is true, that both farmers and merchants must be diligent in their business but not so as to keep them from making religion their main business. <hi type="italic">Licitis perimus omnes—These lawful things undo us,</hi> when they are unlawfully managed, when we are so <hi type="italic">careful and troubled about many things</hi> as to neglect the <hi type="italic">one thing needful.</hi> Observe, Both the city and the country have their temptations, the merchandise in the one, and the farms in the other; so that, whatever we have of the world in our hands, our care must be to keep it out of our hearts, lest it come between us and Christ. <div eID="gen23292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23293" type="x-p"/> 2. The messengers were basely abused; <hi type="italic">The remnant,</hi> or the rest of them, that is, those who did not go the <hi type="italic">farms,</hi> or <hi type="italic">merchandise,</hi> were neither husbandmen nor tradesmen, but ecclesiastics, <hi type="italic">the scribes, and Pharisees, and chief priests;</hi> these were the persecutors, these <hi type="italic">took the servants, and treated them spitefully, and slew them.</hi> This, in the parable, is unaccountable, never any could be so rude and barbarous as this, to servants that came to invite them to a feast; but, in the application of the parable, it was matter of fact; they whose <hi type="italic">feet</hi> should have been <hi type="italic">beautiful,</hi> because they brought <hi type="italic">the glad tidings of the solemn feasts</hi> (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.15">Nahum i. 15</reference>), were <hi type="italic">treated as the offscouring of all things,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.13">1 Cor. iv. 13</reference>. The prophets and John the Baptist had been thus abused already, and the apostles and ministers of Christ must count upon the same. The Jews were, either directly or indirectly, agents in most of the persecutions of the first preachers of the gospel; witness the history of <hi type="italic">the Acts,</hi> that is, the sufferings <hi type="italic">of the apostles.</hi> <div eID="gen23293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23294" type="x-p"/> IV. The utter ruin that was coming upon the Jewish church and nation is here represented by the revenge which the king, in wrath, took on these insolent recusants (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.7">v. 7</reference>); <hi type="italic">He was wroth.</hi> The Jews, who had been the people of God's love and blessing, by rejecting the gospel became the generation of his wrath and curse. <hi type="italic">Wrath came upon them to the uttermost,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.16">1 Thess. ii. 16</reference>. Now observe here, <div eID="gen23294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23295" type="x-p"/> 1. What was the crying sin that brought the ruin; it was their being <hi type="italic">murderers.</hi> He does not say, he destroyed those <hi type="italic">despisers of his call,</hi> but <hi type="italic">those murderers of his servants;</hi> as if God were more jealous for the lives of his ministers than for the honour of his gospel; he that <hi type="italic">toucheth them, toucheth the apple of his eye.</hi> Note, Persecution of Christ's faithful ministers fills the measure of guilt more than any thing. <hi type="italic">Filling Jerusalem with innocent blood</hi> was that sin of Manasseh which <hi type="italic">the Lord would not pardon,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.4">2 Kings xxiv. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen23295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23296" type="x-p"/> 2. What was the ruin itself, that was coming; <hi type="italic">He sent forth his armies.</hi> The Roman armies were his armies, of his raising, of his sending against the people of his wrath; and he <hi type="italic">gave them a charge to tread them down,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.10.6">Isa. x. 6</reference>. God is the Lord of men's host, and makes what use he pleases of them, to serve his own purposes, though they <hi type="italic">mean not so, neither doth their heart think so,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.10.7">Isa. x. 7</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Mic.4.11-Mic.4.12">Mic. iv. 11, 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">His armies destroyed those murderers, and burnt up their city.</hi> This points out very plainly the destruction of the Jews, and the burning of Jerusalem, by the Romans, forty years after this. No age ever saw a greater desolation than that, nor more of the direful effects of fire and sword. Though Jerusalem had been a <hi type="italic">holy city, the city that God had chosen, to put his name there, beautiful for situation, the joy of the whole earth;</hi> yet that city being now <hi type="italic">become a harlot, righteousness being no longer lodged in it, but murderers, the worst of murderers</hi> (as the prophet speaks, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.21">Isa. i. 21</reference>), judgment came upon it, and ruin without remedy; and it is set forth for an example to all that should oppose Christ and his gospel. It was the Lord's doing, to avenge the quarrel of his covenant. <div eID="gen23296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23297" type="x-p"/> V. The replenishing of the church again, by the bringing in of the Gentiles, is here represented by the furnishing of the feast with guests <hi type="italic">out of the high-ways,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.22.8-Matt.22.10">v. 8-10</reference>. <div eID="gen23297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23298" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The complaint of the master of the feast concerning those that were first bidden (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.8">v. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">The wedding is ready,</hi> the covenant of grace ready to be sealed, a church ready to be founded; <hi type="italic">but they which were bidden,</hi> that is, the Jews, <hi type="italic">to whom pertained the covenant and the promises,</hi> by which they were of old invited to the <hi type="italic">feast of fat things,</hi> they <hi type="italic">were not worthy,</hi> they were utterly unworthy, and, by their contempt of Christ, had forfeited all the privileges they were invited to. Note, It is not owing to God, that sinners perish, but to themselves. Thus, when Israel of old was within sight of Canaan, the land of promise was ready, the milk and honey ready, but their unbelief and murmuring, and contempt of that pleasant land, shut them out, and their carcases were left to perish in the wilderness; and <hi type="italic">these things happened to them for ensamples.</hi> See <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.11">1 Cor. x. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.3.16-Heb.4.1">Heb. iii. 16-iv. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen23298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23299" type="x-p"/> 2. The commission he gave to the servants, to invite other guests. The inhabitants of the <hi type="italic">city</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.7">v. 7</reference>) had refused; <hi type="italic">Go into the high-ways</hi> then; into <hi type="italic">the way of the Gentiles,</hi> which at first they were to decline, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.5">ch. x. 5</reference>. Thus by the fall of the Jews salvation is come to the Gentiles, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.11-Rom.11.12">Rom. xi. 11, 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.8">Eph. iii. 8</reference>. Note, Christ will have a <hi type="italic">kingdom in the world,</hi> though many reject the grace, and resist the power, of that kingdom. <hi type="italic">Though Israel be not gathered, he will be glorious.</hi> The offer of Christ and salvation to the Gentiles was, (1.) Unlooked for and unexpected; such a surprise as it would be to wayfaring men upon the road to be met with an invitation to a wedding feast. The Jews had notice of the gospel, long before, and expected the Messiah and his kingdom; but to the Gentiles it was all new, what they had never heard of before (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.19-Acts.17.20">Acts xvii. 19, 20</reference>), and, consequently, what they could not conceive of as belonging to them. See <reference osisRef="Isa.65.1-Isa.65.2">Isa. lxv. 1, 2</reference>. (2.) It was universal and undistinguishing; <hi type="italic">Go, and bid as many as you find.</hi> The highways are public places, and there <hi type="italic">Wisdom cries,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.1.20">Prov. i. 20</reference>. "Ask them that go by the way, ask any body (<reference osisRef="Job.21.29">Job xxi. 29</reference>), high and low, rich and poor, bond and free, young and old, Jew and Gentile; tell them all, that they shall be welcome to gospel-privileges upon gospel-terms; whoever will, let him come, without exception." <div eID="gen23299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23300" type="x-p"/> 3. The success of this second invitation; if some will not come, others will (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.10">v. 10</reference>); <hi type="italic">They gathered together all, as many as they found.</hi> The servants obeyed their orders. Jonah was sent <hi type="italic">into the high-ways,</hi> but was so tender of the honour of his country, that he avoided the errand; but Christ's apostles, though Jews, preferred the service of Christ before their respect to their nation; and St. Paul, though sorrowing for the Jews, yet magnifies his office as the apostle of Gentiles. <hi type="italic">They gathered together all.</hi> The design of the gospel is, (1.) To gather souls together; not the nation of the Jews only, but <hi type="italic">all the children of God</hi> who were <hi type="italic">scattered abroad</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.11.52">John xi. 52</reference>), <hi type="italic">the other sheep that were not of that fold,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.10.16">John x. 16</reference>. They were gathered into one body, one family, one corporation. (2.) To gather them together to the wedding-feast, to pay their respect to Christ, and to partake of the privileges of the new covenant. Where the dole is, there will the poor be gathered together. <div eID="gen23300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23301" type="x-p"/> Now the guests that were gathered were, [1.] A multitude, <hi type="italic">all, as many as they found;</hi> so many, that the guest-chamber was filled. The sealed ones of the Jews were numbered, but those of other nations <hi type="italic">were without number, a very great multitude,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.7.9">Rev. vii. 9</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Isa.60.4">Isa. lx. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.60.8">8</reference>. [2.] A mixed multitude, <hi type="italic">both bad and good;</hi> some that before their conversion were sober and well-inclined, as the devout Greeks (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.4">Acts xvii. 4</reference>) and Cornelius; others that had run to an excess of riot, as the Corinthians (<reference osisRef="1Cor.6.11">1 Cor. vi. 11</reference>); <hi type="italic">Such were some of you;</hi> or, some that after their conversion proved bad, that <hi type="italic">turned not to the Lord with all their heart,</hi> but feignedly; others that were upright and sincere, and proved of the right class. Ministers, in casting the net of the gospel, enclose <hi type="italic">both good</hi> fish <hi type="italic">and bad;</hi> <hi type="italic">but the Lord knows them that are his.</hi> <div eID="gen23301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23302" type="x-p"/> VI. The case of hypocrites, who are <hi type="italic">in</hi> the church, but not <hi type="italic">of</hi> it, who have a name to live, but are not alive indeed, is represented by <hi type="italic">the guest that had not on a wedding garment;</hi> one of the bad that were gathered in. Those come short of salvation by Christ, not only who refuse to take upon them the profession of religion, but who are not sound at heart in that profession. Concerning this hypocrite observe, <div eID="gen23302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23303" type="x-p"/> 1. His discovery, how he was found out, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.11">v. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen23303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23304" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">The king came in to see the guests,</hi> to bid those welcome who came prepared, and to turn those out who came otherwise. Note, The God of heaven takes particular notice of those who profess religion, and have a place and name in the visible church. Our Lord Jesus <hi type="italic">walks among the golden candlesticks</hi> and therefore <hi type="italic">knows their works.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Rev.2.1-Rev.2.2">Rev. ii. 1, 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.7.12">Cant. vii. 12</reference>. Let this be a warning to us against hypocrisy, that disguises will shortly be stripped off, and every man will appear in his own colours; and an encouragement to us in our sincerity, that God is a witness to it. <div eID="gen23304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23305" type="x-p"/> Observe, This hypocrite was never discovered to be without <hi type="italic">a wedding garment,</hi> till <hi type="italic">the king himself came in to see the guests.</hi> Note, It is God's prerogative to know who are sound at heart in their profession, and who are not. We may be deceived in men, either one way or other; but He cannot. The day of judgment will be the great discovering day, when all the guests will be presented to the King: then <hi type="italic">he will separate between the precious and the vile</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.32">ch. xxv. 32</reference>), <hi type="italic">the secrets of all hearts will then be made manifest,</hi> and we shall infallibly discern <hi type="italic">between the righteous and the wicked,</hi> which now it is not easy to do. It concerns all the guests, to prepare for the scrutiny, and to consider how they will pass the piercing eye of the heart-searching God. <div eID="gen23305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23306" type="x-p"/> (2.) As soon as he came in, he presently espied the hypocrite; <hi type="italic">He saw there a man which had not on a wedding garment;</hi> though but one, he soon had his eye upon him; there is no hope of being hid in a crowd from the arrests of divine justice; he had not on a wedding garment; he was not dressed as became a nuptial solemnity; he had not his best clothes on. Note, Many come to the wedding feast without a wedding garment. If the gospel be the wedding feast, then the wedding garment is a frame of heart, and a course of life agreeable to the gospel and our profession of it, <hi type="italic">worthy of the vocation wherewith we are called</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.1">Eph. iv. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">as becomes the gospel of Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.1.27">Phil. i. 27</reference>. <hi type="italic">The righteousness of saints,</hi> their real holiness and sanctification, and Christ, <hi type="italic">made Righteousness to them, is the clean linen,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.19.8">Rev. xix. 8</reference>. This man was not naked, or in rags; some raiment he had, but not a wedding garment. Those, and those only, who <hi type="italic">put on the Lord Jesus,</hi> that have a Christian temper of mind, and are adorned with Christian graces, who live by faith in Christ, and to whom he is all in all, have the wedding garment. <div eID="gen23306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23307" type="x-p"/> 2. His trial (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.12">v. 12</reference>); and here we may observe, <div eID="gen23307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23308" type="x-p"/> (1.) How he was arraigned (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.12">v. 12</reference>); <hi type="italic">Friend, how camest thou in hither, not having a wedding garment?</hi> A startling question to one that was priding himself in the place he securely possessed at the feast. <hi type="italic">Friend!</hi> That was a cutting word; a seeming friend, a pretended friend, a friend in profession, under manifold ties and obligations to be a friend. Note, There are many in the church who are false friends to Jesus Christ, who say that they love him while their hearts are not with him. <hi type="italic">How camest thou in hither?</hi> He does not chide the servants for letting him in (the wedding garment is an inward thing, ministers must go according to that which falls within their cognizance); but he checks his presumption in crowding in, when he knew that his heart was not upright; "How durst thou claim a share in gospel benefits, when thou hadst no regard to gospel rules? <hi type="italic">What has thou to do to declare my statutes?</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.50.16-Ps.50.17">Ps. l. 16, 17</reference>. Such are spots in the feast, dishonour the bridegroom, affront the company, and disgrace themselves; and therefore, <hi type="italic">How camest thou in hither?</hi> Note, The day is coming, when hypocrites will be called to an account for all their presumptuous intrusion into gospel ordinances, and usurpation of gospel privileges. <hi type="italic">Who hath required this at your hand?</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.1.12">Isa. i. 12</reference>. Despised sabbaths and abused sacraments must be reckoned for, and judgment taken out upon an action of waste against all those who <hi type="italic">received the grace of God in vain.</hi> "How camest thou to the Lord's table, at such a time, unhumbled and unsanctified? What brought thee to sit before God's prophets, as his people do, when thy heart went after thy covetousness? <hi type="italic">How camest thou in?</hi> Not by the door, but <hi type="italic">some other way, as a thief and a robber.</hi> It was a tortuous entry, a possession without colour of a title." Note, It is good for those that have a place in the church, often to put it to themselves, "How came I in hither? Have I a wedding-garment?" If we would thus <hi type="italic">judge ourselves, we should not be judged.</hi> <div eID="gen23308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23309" type="x-p"/> (2.) How he was convicted; <hi type="italic">he was speechless:</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ephimothe</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">he was muzzled</hi> (so the word is used, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.9">1 Cor. ix. 9</reference>); the man stood mute, upon his arraignment, being convicted and condemned by his own conscience. They who live within the church, and die without Christ, will not have one word to say for themselves in the judgment of the great day, they will be without excuse; should they plead, <hi type="italic">We have eaten and drunk in thy presence,</hi> as they do, <reference osisRef="Luke.13.26">Luke xiii. 26</reference>, that is to plead guilty; for the crime they are charged with, is thrusting themselves into the presence of Christ, and to his table, before they were called. They who never heard a word of this wedding feast will have more to say for themselves; their sin will be more excusable, and their condemnation more tolerable, than theirs who came to the feast without the wedding garment, and so sin against the clearest light and dearest love. <div eID="gen23309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23310" type="x-p"/> 3. His sentence (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.13">v. 13</reference>); <hi type="italic">Bind him hand and foot,</hi> &c. <div eID="gen23310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23311" type="x-p"/> (1.) He is ordered to be pinioned, as condemned malefactors are, to be manacled and shackled. Those that will not work and walk as they should, may expect to be bound hand and foot. There is a binding in this world by the servants, the ministers, whose suspending of persons that walk disorderly, to the scandal of religion, is called binding of them, <reference osisRef="Matt.18.18">ch. xviii. 18</reference>. "Bind them up from partaking of special ordinances, and the peculiar privileges of their church-membership; bind them over to the righteous judgment of god." <hi type="italic">In the day of judgment,</hi> hypocrites will be bound; <hi type="italic">the angels shall bind up these tares in bundles for the fire,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.13.41">ch. xiii. 41</reference>. Damned sinners are bound hand and foot by an irreversible sentence; this signifies the same with the fixing of the great gulf; they can neither resist nor outrun their punishment. <div eID="gen23311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23312" type="x-p"/> (2.) He is ordered to be carried off from the wedding feast; <hi type="italic">Take him away.</hi> When the wickedness of hypocrites appears, they are to be taken away from the communion of the faithful, to be cut of as withered branches. This bespeaks the punishment of loss in the other world; they shall be taken away from the king, from the kingdom, from the wedding feast, <hi type="italic">Depart from me, ye cursed.</hi> It will aggravate their misery, that (like the unbelieving lord, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.7.2">2 Kings vii. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">they shall see all this plenty with their eyes, but shall not taste of it.</hi> Note, Those that walk unworthy of their Christianity, forfeit all the happiness they presumptuously laid claim to, and complimented themselves with a groundless expectation of. <div eID="gen23312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23313" type="x-p"/> (3.) He is ordered into a doleful dungeon; <hi type="italic">Cast him into utter darkness.</hi> Our Saviour here insensibly slides out of this parable into that which it intimates—the damnation of hypocrites in the other world. Hell is utter darkness, it is darkness out of heaven, the land of light; or it is extreme darkness, darkness to the last degree, without the least ray or spark of light, or hope of it, like that of Egypt; <hi type="italic">darkness which might be felt; the blackness of darkness, as darkness itself,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.10.22">Job x. 22</reference>. Note, Hypocrites go by the light of the gospel itself down to utter darkness; and hell will be hell indeed to such, a condemnation more intolerable; <hi type="italic">there shall be weeping, and gnashing of teeth.</hi> This our Saviour often uses as part of the description of hell-torments, which are hereby represented, not so much by the misery itself, as by the resentment sinners will have of it; there shall be <hi type="italic">weeping,</hi> an expression of great sorrow and anguish; not a gush of tears, which gives present ease, but constant weeping, which is constant torment; and the <hi type="italic">gnashing of teeth</hi> is an expression of the greatest rage and indignation; they will be <hi type="italic">like a wild bull in a net, full of the fury of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.51.20">Isa. li. 20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.21-Isa.8.22">viii. 21, 22</reference>. Let us therefore hear and fear. <div eID="gen23313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23314" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> The parable is concluded with that remarkable saying which we had before (<reference osisRef="Matt.20.16">ch. xx. 16</reference>), <hi type="italic">Many are called, but few are chosen,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.22.14">v. 14</reference>. Of the many that are called to the wedding feast, if you set aside all those as unchosen that make light of it, and avowedly prefer other things before it; if then you set aside all that make a profession of religion, but the temper of whose spirits and the tenour of whose conversation are a constant contradiction to it; if you set aside all the profane, and all the hypocritical, you will find that they are few, very few, that are chosen; many called to the wedding feast, but few chosen to the wedding garment, that is, to <hi type="italic">salvation, by sanctification of the Spirit.</hi> This <hi type="italic">is the strait gate, and narrow way,</hi> which <hi type="italic">few find.</hi>
entries.7b3fd3412000166b570c4b5a2e9ce28990b54418: <div eID="gen23314" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Question Respecting Tribute.</title> <div sID="gen23315" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> Then went the Pharisees, and took counsel how they might entangle him in <hi type="italic">his</hi> talk. <hi type="super">16</hi> And they sent out unto him their disciples with the Herodians, saying, Master, we know that thou art true, and teachest the way of God in truth, neither carest thou for any <hi type="italic">man:</hi> for thou regardest not the person of men. <hi type="super">17</hi> Tell us therefore, What thinkest thou? Is it lawful to give tribute unto Caesar, or not? <hi type="super">18</hi> But Jesus perceived their wickedness, and said, Why tempt ye me, <hi type="italic">ye</hi> hypocrites? <hi type="super">19</hi> show me the tribute money. And they brought unto him a penny. <hi type="super">20</hi> And he saith unto them, Whose <hi type="italic">is</hi> this image and superscription? <hi type="super">21</hi> They say unto him, Caesar's. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's. 22 When they had heard <hi type="italic">these words,</hi> they marvelled, and left him, and went their way. <div eID="gen23315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23316" type="x-p"/> It was not the least grievous of the sufferings of Christ, that <hi type="italic">he endured the contradiction of sinners against himself,</hi> and had snares laid for him by those that sought how to take him off with some pretence. In these verses, we have him attacked by the Pharisees and Herodians with a question about paying tribute to Cæsar. Observe, <div eID="gen23316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23317" type="x-p"/> I. What the design was, which they proposed to themselves; <hi type="italic">They took counsel to entangle him in his talk.</hi> Hitherto, his encounters had been mostly with the chief priests and the elders, men in authority, who trusted more to their power than to their policy, and examined him concerning his commission (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.23">ch. xxi. 23</reference>); but now he is set upon from another quarter; the Pharisees will try whether they can deal with him by their learning in the law, and in casuistical divinity, and they have a <hi type="italic">tentamen novum—a new trial</hi> for him. Note, It is in vain for the best and wisest of men to think that, by their ingenuity, or interest, or industry, or even by their innocence and integrity, they can escape the hatred and ill will of bad men, or screen themselves from <hi type="italic">the strife of tongues.</hi> See how unwearied the enemies of Christ and his kingdom are in their opposition! <div eID="gen23317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23318" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">They took counsel.</hi> It was foretold concerning him, that <hi type="italic">the rulers</hi> would <hi type="italic">take counsel against him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.2">Ps. ii. 2</reference>); and <hi type="italic">so persecuted they the prophets. Come, and let us devise devices against Jeremiah.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Jer.18.18">Jer. xviii. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.20.10">xx. 10</reference>. Note, The more there is of contrivance and consultation about sin, the worse it is. There is a particular <hi type="italic">woe to them that devise iniquity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.2.1">Mic. ii. 1</reference>. The more there is of the wicked wit in the contrivance of a sin, the more there is of the wicked will in the commission of it. <div eID="gen23318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23319" type="x-p"/> 2. That which they aimed at was <hi type="italic">to entangle him in his talk.</hi> They saw him free and bold in speaking his mind, and hoped by that, if they could bring him to some nice and tender point, to get an advantage against him. It has been the old practice of Satan's agents and emissaries, to make a man an offender for a word, a word misplaced, or mistaken, or misunderstood; a word, though innocently designed, yet perverted by strained inuendos: thus they lay a snare for him that <hi type="italic">reproveth in the gate</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.21">Isa. xxix. 21</reference>), and represent the greatest teachers as the greatest troublers of Israel: thus <hi type="italic">the wicked plotteth against the just,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.37.12-Ps.37.13">Ps. xxxvii. 12, 13</reference>. <div eID="gen23319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23320" type="x-p"/> There are two ways by which the enemies of Christ might be revenged on him, and be rid of him; either by law or by force. By law they could not do it, unless they could make him obnoxious to the civil government; for <hi type="italic">it was not lawful for them to put any man to death</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.18.31">John xviii. 31</reference>); and the Roman powers were not apt to concern themselves about <hi type="italic">questions of words, and names, and their law,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.18.15">Acts xviii. 15</reference>. By force they could not do it, unless they could make him obnoxious to the people, who were always the hands, whoever were the heads, in such acts of violence, which they call the beating of the rebels; but the people took Christ for a Prophet, and therefore his enemies could not raise the mob against him. Now (as the old serpent was from the beginning <hi type="italic">more subtle than any beast of the field</hi>), the design was, to bring him into such a dilemma, that he must make himself liable to the displeasure either of the Jewish multitude, or of the Roman magistrates; let him take which side of the question he will, he shall run himself into a premunire; and so they will gain their point, and make his own tongue to fall upon him. <div eID="gen23320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23321" type="x-p"/> II. The question which they put to him pursuant to this design, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.16-Matt.22.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. Having devised this iniquity in secret, in a close cabal, behind the curtain, when they went abroad without loss of time they practised it. Observe, <div eID="gen23321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23322" type="x-p"/> 1. The persons they employed; they did not go themselves, lest the design should be suspected and Christ should stand the more upon his guard; but they sent their disciples, who would look less like tempters, and more like learners. Note, Wicked men will never want wicked instruments to be employed in carrying on their wicked counsels. Pharisees have their disciples at their beck, who will go any errand for them, and say as they say; and they have this in their eyes, when they are so industrious to make proselytes. <div eID="gen23322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23323" type="x-p"/> With them they sent the Herodians, a party among the Jews, who were for a cheerful and entire subjection to the Roman emperor, and to Herod his deputy; and who made it their business to reconcile people to that government, and pressed all to pay their tribute. Some think that they were the collectors of the land tax, as the publicans were of the customs, and that they went with the Pharisees to Christ, with this blind upon their plot, that while the Herodians demanded the tax, and the Pharisees denied it, they were both willing to refer it to Christ, as a proper Judge to decide the quarrel. Herod being obliged, by the charter of the sovereignty, to take care of the tribute, these Herodians, by assisting him in that, helped to endear him to his great friends at Rome. The Pharisees, on the other hand, were zealous for the liberty of the Jews, and did what they could to make them impatient of the Roman yoke. Now, if he should countenance the paying of tribute, the Pharisees would incense the people against him; if he should discountenance or disallow it, the Herodians would incense the government against him. Note, It is common for those that oppose one another, to continue in an opposition to Christ and his kingdom. Samson's foxes looked several ways, but met in one firebrand. See <reference osisRef="Ps.83.3">Ps. lxxxiii. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.83.5">5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.83.7">7,</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.83.8">8</reference>. If they are unanimous in opposing, should not we be so in maintaining, the interests of the gospel? <div eID="gen23323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23324" type="x-p"/> 2. The preface, with which they were plausibly to introduce the question; it was highly complimentary to our Saviour (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.16">v. 16</reference>); <hi type="italic">Master, we know that thou art true, and teachest the way of God in truth.</hi> Note, It is a common thing for the most spiteful projects to be covered with the most specious pretences. Had they come to Christ with the most serious enquiry, and the most sincere intention, they could not have expressed themselves better. Here is <hi type="italic">hatred covered with deceit,</hi> and a <hi type="italic">wicked heart with burning lips</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.26.23">Prov. xxvi. 23</reference>); as Judas, who kissed, and betrayed, as Joab, who kissed, and killed. <div eID="gen23324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23325" type="x-p"/> Now, (1.) What they said of Christ was right, and whether they knew it or no, blessed be God, we know it. <div eID="gen23325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23326" type="x-p"/> [1.] That Jesus Christ was a faithful Teacher; <hi type="italic">Thou art true, and teachest the way of God in truth.</hi> For himself, <hi type="italic">he is true, the Amen, the faithful Witness;</hi> he is the Truth itself. As for his doctrine, the matter of his teaching was the way of God, the way that God requires us to walk in, the way of duty, that leads to happiness; that is the way of God. The manner of it was in truth; he showed people <hi type="italic">the right way, the way in which they should go.</hi> He was a skilful Teacher, and knew the way of God; and a faithful Teacher, that would be sure to let us know it. See <reference osisRef="Prov.8.6-Prov.8.9">Prov. viii. 6-9</reference>. This is the character of a good teacher, to preach the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and not to suppress, pervert, or stretch, any truth, for favour or affection, hatred or good will, either out of a desire to please, or a fear to offend, any man. <div eID="gen23326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23327" type="x-p"/> [2.] That he was a bold Reprover. In preaching, he <hi type="italic">cared not for any;</hi> he valued no man's frowns or smiles, he did not court, he did not dread, either the great or the many, for he <hi type="italic">regarded not the person of man.</hi> In his evangelical judgment, he did not know faces; that <hi type="italic">Lion of the tribe of Judah, turned not away for any</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.30">Prov. xxx. 30</reference>), turned not a step from the truth, nor from his work, for fear of the most formidable. He <hi type="italic">reproved with equity</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">Isa. xi. 4</reference>), and never with partiality. <div eID="gen23327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23328" type="x-p"/> (2.) Though what they said was true for the matter of it, yet there was nothing but flattery and treachery in the intention of it. They called him <hi type="italic">Master,</hi> when they were contriving to treat him as the worst of malefactors; they pretended respect for him, when they intended mischief against him; and they affronted his wisdom as Man, much more his omniscience as God, of which he had so often given undeniable proofs, when they imagined that they could impose upon him with these pretences, and that he could not see through them. It is the grossest atheism, that is the greatest folly in the world, to think to put a cheat upon Christ, who searches the heart, <reference osisRef="Rev.2.23">Rev. ii. 23</reference>. Those that mock God do but deceive themselves. <reference osisRef="Gal.6.7">Gal. vi. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen23328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23329" type="x-p"/> 3. The proposal of the case; <hi type="italic">What thinkest thou?</hi> As if they had said, "Many men are of many minds in this matter; it is a case which relates to practice, and occurs daily; let us have thy thought freely in the matter, <hi type="italic">Is it lawful to give tribute to Cæsar or not?</hi>" This implies a further question; Has Cæsar a right to demand it? The nation of the Jews was lately, about a hundred years before this, conquered by the Roman sword, and so, as other nations, made subject to the Roman yoke, and became a province of the empire; accordingly, toll, tribute, and custom, were demanded from them, and sometimes poll-money. By this it appeared that <hi type="italic">the sceptre was departed from Judah</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen. xlix. 10</reference>); and therefore, if they had understood the signs of the times, they must have concluded that <hi type="italic">Shiloh was come,</hi> and either that this was he, or they must find out another more likely to be so. <div eID="gen23329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23330" type="x-p"/> Now the question was, Whether it was lawful to pay these taxes voluntarily, or, Whether they should not insist upon the ancient liberty of their nation, and rather suffer themselves to be distrained upon? The ground of the doubt was, that they <hi type="italic">were Abraham's seed,</hi> and should not by consent be <hi type="italic">in bondage to any man,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.8.33">John viii. 33</reference>. God had given them a law, that they should not <hi type="italic">set a stranger over them.</hi> Did not that imply, that they were not to yield any willing subjection to any prince, state, or potentate, that was not of their own nation and religion? This was an old mistake, arising from that <hi type="italic">pride and</hi> that <hi type="italic">haughty spirit</hi> which bring <hi type="italic">destruction and a fall.</hi> Jeremiah, in his time, though he spoke in God's name, could not possibly beat them off it, nor persuade them to submit to the king of Babylon; and their obstinacy in that matter was then their ruin (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.12-Jer.27.13">Jer. xxvii. 12, 13</reference>): and now again they stumbled at the same stone; and it was the very thing which, in a few years after, brought final destruction upon them by the Romans. They quite mistook the sense both of the precept and of the privilege, and, under colour of God's word, contended with his providence, when they should have kissed the rod, and accepted the punishment of their iniquity. <div eID="gen23330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23331" type="x-p"/> However, by this question they hoped to entangle Christ, and, which way soever he resolved it, to expose him to the fury either of the jealous Jews, or of the jealous Romans; they were ready to triumph, as Pharaoh did over Israel, that <hi type="italic">the wilderness had shut him in,</hi> and his doctrine would be concluded either injurious to the rights of the church, or hurtful to kings and provinces. <div eID="gen23331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23332" type="x-p"/> III. The breaking of this snare by the wisdom of the Lord Jesus. <div eID="gen23332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23333" type="x-p"/> 1. He discovered it (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.18">v. 18</reference>); <hi type="italic">He perceived their wickedness;</hi> for, <hi type="italic">surely in vain is the net spread in the sight of any bird,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.1.17">Prov. i. 17</reference>. A temptation perceived is half conquered, for our greatest danger lies from snakes under the green grass; <hi type="italic">and he said, Why tempt ye me, ye hypocrites?</hi> Note, Whatever vizard the hypocrite puts on, our Lord Jesus sees through it; he perceives all the wickedness that is in the hearts of pretenders, and can easily convict them of it, and set it in order before them. He cannot be imposed upon, as we often are, by flatteries and fair pretences. He that searches the heart can call hypocrites by their own name, as Ahijah did the wife of Jeroboam (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.6">1 Kings xiv. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">Why feignest thou thyself to be another? Why tempt ye me, ye hypocrites?</hi> Note, Hypocrites tempt Jesus Christ; they try his knowledge, whether he can discover them through their disguises; they try his holiness and truth, whether he will allow of them in this church; but if they that of old <hi type="italic">tempted Christ,</hi> when he was but darkly revealed, <hi type="italic">were destroyed of serpents, of how much sorer punishment shall they be thought worthy</hi> who tempt him now in the midst of gospel light and love! Those that presume to tempt Christ will certainly find him too hard for them, and that he is of more piercing eyes than not to see, and more pure eyes than not to hate, the disguised wickedness of hypocrites, that dig deep to hide their counsel from him. <div eID="gen23333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23334" type="x-p"/> 2. He evaded it; his convicting them of hypocrisy might have served for an answer (such captious malicious questions deserve a reproof, not a reply): but our Lord Jesus gave a full answer to their question, and introduced it by an argument sufficient to support it, so as to lay down a rule for his church in this matter, and yet to avoid giving offence, and to break the snare. <div eID="gen23334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23335" type="x-p"/> (1.) He forced them, ere they were aware, to confess Cæsar's authority over them, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.19-Matt.22.20">v. 19, 20</reference>. In dealing with those that are captious, it is good to give our reasons, and, if possible, reasons of confessed cogency, before we give our resolutions. Thus the evidence of truth may silence gainsayers by surprise, while they only stood upon their guard against the truth itself, not against the reason of it; <hi type="italic">Show me the tribute-money.</hi> He had none of his own to convince them by; it should seem, he had not so much as one piece of money about him, for for our sakes he emptied himself, and became poor; he despised the wealth of this world, and thereby taught us not to over-value it; silver and gold he had none; why then should we covet to load ourselves with the thick clay? The Romans demanded their tribute in their own money, which was current among the Jews at that time: that therefore is called the <hi type="italic">tribute-money;</hi> he does not name what piece but the <hi type="italic">tribute money,</hi> to show that he did not mind things of that nature, nor concern himself about them; his heart was upon better things, the kingdom of God and the riches and righteousness thereof, and ours should be so too. They presently <hi type="italic">brought him a penny,</hi> a Roman penny in silver, in value about sevenpence half-penny of our money, the most common piece then in use: it was stamped with the emperor's image and superscription, which was the warrant of the public faith for the value of the pieces so stamped; a method agreed on by most nations, for the more easy circulation of money with satisfaction. The coining of money has always been looked upon as a branch of the prerogative, a flower of the crown, a royalty belonging to the sovereign powers; and the admitting of that as the good and lawful money of a country is an implicit submission to those powers, and an owning of them in money matters. How happy is our constitution, and how happy we, who live in a nation where, though the image and superscription be the sovereign's, the property is the subject's, under the protection of the laws, and what we have we can call our own! <div eID="gen23335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23336" type="x-p"/> Christ asked them, <hi type="italic">Whose image is this?</hi> They owned it to be Cæsar's, and thereby convicted those of falsehood who said, <hi type="italic">We were never in bondage to any;</hi> and confirmed what afterward they said, <hi type="italic">We have no king but Cæsar.</hi> It is a rule in the Jewish Talmud, that "he is the king of the country whose coin is current in the country." Some think that the superscription upon this coin was a memorandum of the conquest of Judea by the Romans, <hi type="italic">anno post captam Judæam—the year after that event;</hi> and that they admitted that too. <div eID="gen23336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23337" type="x-p"/> (2.) From thence he inferred the lawfulness of paying tribute to Cæsar (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.21">v. 21</reference>); <hi type="italic">Render therefore to Cæsar the things that are Cæsar's;</hi> not, "<hi type="italic">Give</hi> it him" (as they expressed it, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.17">v. 17</reference>), but, "<hi type="italic">Render</hi> it; Return," or "Restore it; if Cæsar fill the purses, let Cæsar command them. It is too late now to dispute paying tribute to Cæsar; for you are become a province of the empire, and, when once a relation is admitted, the duty of it must be performed. <hi type="italic">Render to all their due,</hi> and particularly <hi type="italic">tribute to whom tribute is due.</hi>" Now by this answer, <div eID="gen23337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23338" type="x-p"/> [1.] No offence was given. It was much to the honour of Christ and his doctrine, that he did not interpose as a Judge or a Divider in matters of this nature, but left them as he found them, for <hi type="italic">his kingdom is not of this world;</hi> and in this he hath given an example to his ministers, who deal in sacred things, not to meddle with disputes about things secular, not to wade far into controversies relating to them, but to leave that to those whose proper business it is. Ministers that would mind their business, and please their master, must not <hi type="italic">entangle themselves in the affairs of this life:</hi> they forfeit the guidance of God's Spirit, and the convoy of his providence when they thus go out of their way. Christ discusses not the emperor's title, but enjoins a peaceable subjection to <hi type="italic">the powers that be.</hi> The government therefore had no reason to take offence at his determination, but to thank him, for it would strengthen Cæsar's interest with the people, who held him for a Prophet; and yet such was the impudence of his prosecutors, that, though he had expressly charged them to <hi type="italic">render to Cæsar the things that are Cæsar's,</hi> they laid the direct contrary in his indictment, that he <hi type="italic">forbade to give tribute to Cæsar,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.23.2">Luke xxiii. 2</reference>. As to the people, the Pharisees could not accuse him to them, because they themselves had, before they were aware, yielded the premises, and then it was too late to evade the conclusion. Note, Though truth seeks not a fraudulent concealment, yet it sometimes needs a prudent management, to prevent the offence which may be taken at it. <div eID="gen23338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23339" type="x-p"/> [2.] His adversaries were reproved. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Some of them would have had him make it unlawful to give tribute to Cæsar, that they might have a pretence to save their money. Thus many excuse themselves from that which they must do, by arguing whether they may do it or no. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They all withheld from God his dues, and are reproved for that: while they were vainly contending about their civil liberties, they had lost the life and power of religion, and needed to be put in mind of their duty to God, with that to Cæsar. <div eID="gen23339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23340" type="x-p"/> [3.] His disciples were instructed, and standing rules left to the church. <div eID="gen23340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23341" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That the Christian religion is no enemy to civil government, but a friend to it. Christ's kingdom doth not clash or interfere with the kingdoms of the earth, in any thing that pertains to their jurisdiction. By Christ kings reign. <div eID="gen23341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23342" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is the duty of subjects to render to magistrates that which, according to the laws of their country, is their due. The higher powers, being entrusted with the public welfare, the protection of the subject, and the conservation of the peace, are entitled, in consideration thereof, to a just proportion of the public wealth, and the revenue of the nation. <hi type="italic">For this cause pay we tribute,</hi> because <hi type="italic">they attend continually to this very thing</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.13.6">Rom. xiii. 6</reference>); and it is doubtless a greater sin to cheat the government than to cheat a private person. Though it is the constitution that determines what is Cæsar's, yet, when that is determined, Christ bids us render it to him; my coat is my coat, by the law of man; but he is a thief, by the law of God, that takes it from me. <div eID="gen23342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23343" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> When we render to Cæsar the things that are Cæsar's, we must remember withal to render to God the things that are God's. If our purses be Cæsar's, our consciences are God's; he hath said, <hi type="italic">My son, give me thy heart:</hi> he must have the innermost and uppermost place there; we must render to God that which is his due, out of our time and out of our estates; from them he must have his share as well as Cæsar his; and if Cæsar's commands interfere with God's <hi type="italic">we must obey God rather than men.</hi> <div eID="gen23343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23344" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> Observe how they were nonplussed by this answer; they <hi type="italic">marvelled, and left him, and went their way,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.22.22">v. 22</reference>. They admired his sagacity in discovering and evading a snare which they thought so craftily laid. Christ is, and will be, the Wonder, not only of his beloved friends, but of his baffled enemies. One would think they should have marvelled and followed him, marvelled and submitted to him; no, they marvelled and left him. Note, There are many in whose eyes Christ is marvellous, and yet not precious. They admire his wisdom, but will not be guided by it, his power, but will not submit to it. <hi type="italic">They went their way,</hi> as persons ashamed, and made an inglorious retreat. The stratagem being defeated, they quitted the field. Note, There is nothing got by contending with Christ.
entries.af626fbadb9aefe321978dd849534b19cc9559b9: <div eID="gen23344" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Question Respecting Marriage.</title> <div sID="gen23345" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> The same day came to him the Sadducees, which say that there is no resurrection, and asked him, <hi type="super">24</hi> Saying, Master, Moses said, If a man die, having no children, his brother shall marry his wife, and raise up seed unto his brother. <hi type="super">25</hi> Now there were with us seven brethren: and the first, when he had married a wife, deceased, and, having no issue, left his wife unto his brother: <hi type="super">26</hi> Likewise the second also, and the third, unto the seventh. <hi type="super">27</hi> And last of all the woman died also. 28 Therefore in the resurrection whose wife shall she be of the seven? for they all had her. <hi type="super">29</hi> Jesus answered and said unto them, Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God. <hi type="super">30</hi> For in the resurrection they neither marry, nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven. <hi type="super">31</hi> But as touching the resurrection of the dead, have ye not read that which was spoken unto you by God, saying, <hi type="super">32</hi> I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? God is not the God of the dead, but of the living. <hi type="super">33</hi> And when the multitude heard <hi type="italic">this,</hi> they were astonished at his doctrine. <div eID="gen23345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23346" type="x-p"/> We have here Christ's dispute with the Sadducees concerning the resurrection; it was the same day on which he was attacked by the Pharisees about paying tribute. Satan was now more busy than ever to ruffle and disturb him; it was <hi type="italic">an hour of temptation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.10">Rev. iii. 10</reference>. The truth as it is in Jesus will still meet with contradiction, in some branch or other of it. Observe here, <div eID="gen23346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23347" type="x-p"/> I. The opposition which the Sadducees made to a very great truth of religion; they say, <hi type="italic">There is no resurrection,</hi> as there are some fools who say, <hi type="italic">There is no God.</hi> These heretics were called <hi type="italic">Sadducees</hi> from one Sadoc, a disciple of Antigonus Sochæus, who flourished about two hundred and eighty-four years before our Saviour's birth. They lie under heavy censures among the writers of their own nation, as men of base and debauched conversations, which their principles led them to. They were the fewest in number of all the sects among the Jews, but generally persons of some rank. As the Pharisees and Essenes seemed to follow Plato and Pythagoras, so the Sadducees were much of the genius of the Epicureans; they denied the resurrection, they said, There is no future state, no life after this; that, when the body dies, the soul is annihilated, and dies with it; that there is no state of rewards or punishments in the other world; no judgment to come in heaven or hell. They maintained, that, except God, there is not spirit (<reference osisRef="Acts.23.8">Acts xxiii. 8</reference>), nothing but matter and motion. They would not own the divine inspiration of the prophets, nor any revelation from heaven, but what God himself spoke upon mount Sinai. Now the doctrine of Christ carried that great truth of the resurrection and a future state much further than it had yet been revealed, and therefore the Sadducees in a particular manner set themselves against it. The Pharisees and Sadducees were contrary to each other, and yet confederates against Christ. Christ's gospel hath always suffered between superstitious ceremonious hypocrites and bigots on the one hand, and profane deists and infidels on the other. The former abusing, the latter despising, the <hi type="italic">form</hi> of godliness, but both denying the <hi type="italic">power</hi> of it. <div eID="gen23347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23348" type="x-p"/> II. The objection they made against the truth, which was taken from a supposed case of a woman that had seven husbands successively; now they take it for granted, that, if there be a resurrection, it must be a return to such a state as this we are now in, and to the same circumstances, like the imaginary Platonic year; and if so, it is an invincible absurdity for this woman in the future state to have seven husbands, or else an insuperable difficulty which of them should have her, he whom she had first, or he whom she had last, or he whom she loved best, or he whom she lived longest with. <div eID="gen23348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23349" type="x-p"/> 1. They suggest the law of Moses in this matter (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.24">v. 24</reference>), that the next of kin should marry the widow of him that died childless (<reference osisRef="Deut.25.5">Deut. xxv. 5</reference>); we have it practised <reference osisRef="Ruth.4.5">Ruth iv. 5</reference>. It was a political law, founded in the particular constitution of the Jewish commonwealth, to preserve the distinction of families and inheritances, of both which there was special care taken in that government. <div eID="gen23349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23350" type="x-p"/> 2. They put a case upon this statute, which, whether it were a <hi type="italic">case in fact</hi> or only a <hi type="italic">moot case,</hi> is not at all material; if it had not really occurred, yet possibly it might. It was of seven brothers, who married the same woman, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.25-Matt.22.27">v. 25-27</reference>. Now this case supposes, <div eID="gen23350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23351" type="x-p"/> (1.) The desolations that death sometimes makes in families when it comes with commission; how it often sweeps away a whole fraternity in a little time;: seldom (as the case is put) according to seniority (the land of darkness is without any order,) but <hi type="italic">heaps upon heaps;</hi> it diminishes families that had multiplied greatly, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.38-Ps.107.39">Ps. cvii. 38, 39</reference>. When there were seven brothers grown up to man's estate, there was a family very likely to be built up; and yet this numerous family leaves <hi type="italic">neither son nor nephew, nor any remaining in their dwellings,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.18.19">Job xviii. 19</reference>. Well may we say then, <hi type="italic">Except the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it.</hi> Let none be sure of the advancement and perpetuity of their names and families, unless they could <hi type="italic">make a covenant</hi> of peace <hi type="italic">with death,</hi> or be at an <hi type="italic">agreement with the grave.</hi> <div eID="gen23351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23352" type="x-p"/> (2.) The obedience of these seven brothers to the law, though they had a power of refusal under the penalty of a reproach, <reference osisRef="Deut.25.7">Deut. xxv. 7</reference>. Note, Discouraging providences should not keep us from doing our duty because we must be governed by the rule, not by the event. The seventh, who ventured last to marry the widow (many a one would say) was a<hi type="italic">bold</hi> man. I would say, if he did it purely in obedience to God, he was a <hi type="italic">good</hi> man, and one that made conscience of his duty. <div eID="gen23352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23353" type="x-p"/> But, <hi type="italic">last of all, the woman died also.</hi> Note, Survivorship is but a reprieve; they that live long, and bury their relations and neighbours one after another, do not thereby acquire an immortality; no, their day will come to fall. Death's bitter cup goes round, and, sooner or later, we must all pledge in it, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.26">Jer. xxv. 26</reference>. <div eID="gen23353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23354" type="x-p"/> 3. They propose a doubt upon this case (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.28">v. 28</reference>); "<hi type="italic">In the resurrection, whose wife shall she be of the seven?</hi> You cannot tell whose; and therefore we must conclude <hi type="italic">there is no resurrection.</hi>" The Pharisees, who professed to believe a resurrection, had very gross and carnal notions concerning it, and concerning the future state; expecting to find there, as the Turks in their paradise, the delights and pleasures of the animal life, which perhaps drove the Sadducees to deny the thing itself; for nothing gives greater advantage to atheism and infidelity than the carnality of those that make religion, either in its professions or in its prospects, a servant to their sensual appetites and secular interests; while those that are erroneous deny the truth, those that are superstitious betray it to them. Now they, in this objection, went upon the Pharisees' hypothesis. Note, It is not strange that carnal minds have very false notions of spiritual and eternal things. The natural man receiveth not these things, <hi type="italic">for they are foolishness to him.</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.14">1 Cor. ii. 14</reference>. Let truth be set in a clear light, and then it appears in its full strength. <div eID="gen23354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23355" type="x-p"/> III. Christ's answer to this objection; by reproving their ignorance, and rectifying their mistake, he shows the objection to be fallacious and unconcluding. <div eID="gen23355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23356" type="x-p"/> 1. He reproves their ignorance (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.29">v. 29</reference>); <hi type="italic">Ye do err.</hi> Note, Those do greatly err, in the judgment of Christ, who deny the resurrection and a future state. Here Christ reproves with the meekness of wisdom, and is not so sharp upon them (whatever was the reason) as sometimes he was upon the chief priests and elders; <hi type="italic">Ye do err, not knowing.</hi> Note, Ignorance is the cause of error; those that are in the dark, miss their way. The patrons of error do <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> resist the light, and do what they can to take away the key of knowledge; <hi type="italic">Ye do err</hi> in this matter, <hi type="italic">not knowing.</hi> Note, Ignorance is the cause of error about the resurrection and the future state. <hi type="italic">What</hi> it is in its particular instances, the wisest and best know not; it doth not yet appear what we shall be, it is a glory that is to be revealed: when we speak of the state of separate souls, the resurrection of the body, and of eternal happiness and misery, we are soon at a loss; we cannot order our speech, by reason of darkness, but that it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a thing about which we are not left in the dark; blessed be God, we are not; and those who deny it are guilty of a willing and affected ignorance. It seems, there were some Sadducees, some such monsters, among professing Christians, <hi type="italic">some among you, that say, There is no resurrection of the dead</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.12">1 Cor. xv. 12</reference>) and some that did in effect deny it, by turning it into an allegory, saying, The <hi type="italic">resurrection is past already.</hi> Now observe, <div eID="gen23356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23357" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">They know not the power of God;</hi> which would lead men to infer that there <hi type="italic">may be</hi> a resurrection and a future state. Note, The ignorance, disbelief, or weak belief, of God's power, is at the bottom of many errors, particularly theirs who deny the resurrection. When we are told of the soul's existence and agency in a state of separation from the body, and especially that a dead body, which had lain many ages in the grave, and is turned into common and indistinguished dust, that this shall be raised the same body that it was, and live, move, and act, again; we are ready to say, <hi type="italic">How can these things be?</hi> Nature allows it for a maxim, <hi type="italic">A privatione ad habitum non datur regressus—The habits attaching to a state of existence vanish irrecoverably with the state itself.</hi> If a man die, shall he live again? And vain men, because they cannot comprehend the <hi type="italic">way</hi> of it, question the <hi type="italic">truth</hi> of it; whereas, if we firmly believe in God the Father Almighty, that nothing is impossible with God, all these difficulties vanish.
