This therefore we must fasten upon, in the first place, that God is omnipotent, and can do what he will; and then no room is left for doubting but that he will do what he has promised; and, if so, <hi type="italic">why should it be thought a thing incredible with you that God should raise the dead?</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.26.8">Acts xxvi. 8</reference>. His power far exceeds the power of nature. <div eID="gen23357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23358" type="x-p"/> (2.) <hi type="italic">They know not the scriptures,</hi> which decidedly affirm that there shall be a resurrection and a future state. The power of God, determined and engaged by his promise, is the foundation for faith to build upon. Now the scriptures speak plainly, that the soul is immortal, and there is another life after this; it is the scope both of the law and of the prophets, <hi type="italic">that there shall be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and of the unjust,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.24.14-Acts.24.15">Acts xxiv. 14, 15</reference>. Job knew it (<reference osisRef="Job.19.26">Job xix. 26</reference>), Ezekiel foresaw it (<reference osisRef="Ezek.37.1-Ezek.37.28">Ezek. xxxvii.</reference>), and Daniel plainly foretold it, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.2">Dan. xii. 2</reference>. Christ rose again <hi type="italic">according to the scriptures</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.3">1 Cor. xv. 3</reference>); and so shall we. Those therefore who deny it, either have not conversed with the Scriptures, or do not believe them, or do not take the true sense and meaning of them. Note, Ignorance of the scripture is the rise of abundance of mischief. <div eID="gen23358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23359" type="x-p"/> 2. He rectifies their mistake, and (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.30">v. 30</reference>) corrects those gross ideas which they had of the resurrection and a future state, and fixes these doctrines upon a true and lasting basis. Concerning that state, observe, <div eID="gen23359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23360" type="x-p"/> (1.) It is not like the state we are now in upon earth; <hi type="italic">They neither marry, nor are given in marriage.</hi> In our present state marriage is necessary; it was instituted in innocency; whatever intermission or neglect there has been of other institutions, this was never laid aside, nor will be till the end of time. In the old world, they were <hi type="italic">marrying, and giving in marriage;</hi> the Jews in Babylon, when cut off from other ordinances, yet were bid to <hi type="italic">take them wives,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.29.6">Jer. xxix. 6</reference>. All civilized nations have had a sense of the obligation of the marriage covenant; and it is requisite for the gratifying of the desires, and recruiting the deficiencies, of the human nature. But, in the resurrection, there is no occasion for marriage; whether in glorified bodies there will be any distinction of sexes some too curiously dispute (the ancients are divided in their opinions about it); but, whether there will be a distinction or not, it is certain that there will be no conjunction; where God will be <hi type="italic">all in all,</hi> there needs no other <hi type="italic">meet-help;</hi> the body will be <hi type="italic">spiritual,</hi> and there will be in it no carnal desires to be gratified: when the mystical body is completed, there will be no further occasion to <hi type="italic">seek a godly seed,</hi> which was one end of the institution of marriage, <reference osisRef="Mal.2.15">Mal. ii. 15</reference>. In heaven there will be no decay of the individuals, and therefore no eating and drinking; no decay of the species, and therefore no marrying; <hi type="italic">where there shall be no more deaths</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.4">Rev. xxi. 4</reference>), there need be no more births. The married state is a composition of joys and cares; those that enter upon it are taught to look upon it as subject to changes, <hi type="italic">richer and poorer, sickness and health;</hi> and therefore it is fit for this mixed, changing world; but as in hell, where there is no joy, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride shall be heard no more at all, so in heaven, where there is all joy, and no care or pain or trouble, there will be no marrying. The joys of that state are pure and spiritual, and arise from the marriage of all of them to the Lamb, not of any of them to one another. <div eID="gen23360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23361" type="x-p"/> (2.) It is like the state angels are now in in heaven; <hi type="italic">They are as the angels of God in heaven;</hi> they <hi type="italic">are</hi> so, that is, undoubtedly they shall be so. They are so already in Christ their Head, who has made them <hi type="italic">sit with him in heavenly places,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.6">Eph. ii. 6</reference>. The spirits of just men already made perfect are of the same corporation with the innumerable company of angels, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.22-Heb.12.23">Heb. xii. 22, 23</reference>. Man in his creation was <hi type="italic">made a little lower than the angels</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.8.5">Ps. viii. 5</reference>); but in his complete redemption and renovation will be as the angels; pure and spiritual as the angels, knowing and loving as those blessed seraphim, ever praising God like them and with them. The bodies of the saints shall be raised incorruptible and glorious, like the uncompounded vehicles of those pure and holy spirits (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.42">1 Cor. xv. 42</reference>, &c.), swift and strong, like them. We should <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> desire and endeavour to do the will of God now as the angels do it in heaven, because we hope shortly to be like the angels who always behold our Father's face. He saith nothing of the state of the wicked in the resurrection; but, by consequence, they shall be like the devils, whose lusts they have done. <div eID="gen23361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23362" type="x-p"/> IV. Christ's argument to confirm this great truth of the resurrection and a future state; the matters being of great concern, he did not think it enough (as in some other disputes) to discover the fallacy and sophistry of the objection, but backed the truth with a solid argument; for Christ <hi type="italic">brings forth judgment to truth</hi> as well as victory, and enables his followers to give a reason of the hope that is in them. Now observe, <div eID="gen23362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23363" type="x-p"/> 1. Whence he fetched his argument—from the scripture; that is the great magazine or armoury whence we may be furnished with spiritual weapons, offensive and defensive. <hi type="italic">It is written</hi> is Goliath's sword. <hi type="italic">Have ye not read that which was spoken to you by God?</hi> Note, (1.) What the scripture speaks God speaks. (2.) What was spoken to Moses was spoken to us; it was spoken and <hi type="italic">written for our learning.</hi> (3.) It concerns us to read and hear what God hath spoken, because it is spoken to us. It was spoken to you Jews in the first place, for to them were committed the oracles of God. The argument is fetched from the books of Moses, because the Sadducees received <hi type="italic">them</hi> only, as some think, or, at least, them chiefly, for canonical scriptures; Christ therefore fetched his proof from the most indisputable fountain. The latter prophets have more express proofs of a future state than the law of Moses has; for though the law of Moses supposes the immortality of the soul and a future state, as principles of what is called natural religion, yet no express revelation of it is made by the law of Moses; because so much of that law was peculiar to that people, and was therefore guarded as municipal laws used to be with temporal promises and threatenings, and the more express revelation of a future state was reserved for the latter days; but our Saviour finds a very solid argument for the resurrection even in the writings of Moses. Much scripture lies under ground, that must be digged for. <div eID="gen23363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23364" type="x-p"/> 2. What his argument was (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.32">v. 32</reference>); <hi type="italic">I am the God of Abraham.</hi> This was not an express proof, <hi type="italic">totidem verbis—in so many words;</hi> and yet it was really a conclusive argument. Consequences from scripture, if rightly deduced, must be received as scripture; for it was written for those that have the use of reason. <div eID="gen23364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23365" type="x-p"/> Now the drift of the argument is to prove, <div eID="gen23365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23366" type="x-p"/> (1.) That there is a future state, another life after this, in which the righteous shall be truly and constantly happy. This is proved from what God said; <hi type="italic">I am the God of Abraham.</hi> <div eID="gen23366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23367" type="x-p"/> [1.] For God to be any one's God supposes some very extraordinary privilege and happiness; unless we know fully what God is, we could not comprehend the riches of that word, <hi type="italic">I will be to thee a God,</hi> that is, a Benefactor like myself. The God <hi type="italic">of</hi> Israel is a God <hi type="italic">to</hi> Israel (<reference osisRef="1Chr.17.24">1 Chron. xvii. 24</reference>), a spiritual Benefactor; for he is the Father of spirits, and blesseth with spiritual blessings: it is to be an all-sufficient Benefactor, a God that is enough, a complete Good, and an eternal Benefactor; for he is himself an everlasting God, and will be to those that are in covenant with him an everlasting Good. This great word God had often said to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; and it was intended as a recompence for their singular faith and obedience, in quitting the country at God's call. The Jews had a profound veneration for those three patriarchs, and would extend the promise God made them to the uttermost. <div eID="gen23367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23368" type="x-p"/> [2.] It is manifest that these good men had no such extraordinary happiness, in <hi type="italic">this</hi> life, as might look any thing like the accomplishment of so great a word as that. They were strangers in the land of promise, wandering, pinched with famine; they had not a foot of ground of their own but a burying-place, which directed them to look for something beyond this life. In present enjoyments they came far short of their neighbours that were strangers to this covenant. What was there in this world to distinguish them and the heirs of their faith from other people, any whit proportionable to the dignity and distinction of this covenant? If no happiness had been reserved for these great and good men on the other side of death, that melancholy word of poor Jacob's, when he was old (<reference osisRef="Gen.47.9">Gen. xlvii. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">Few and evil have the days of the years of my life been,</hi> would have been an eternal reproach to the wisdom, goodness, and faithfulness, of that God who had so often called himself <hi type="italic">the God of Jacob.</hi> <div eID="gen23368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23369" type="x-p"/> [3.] Therefore there must certainly be a future state, in which, as God will ever live to be eternally rewarding, so Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, will ever live to be eternally rewarded. That of the apostle (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.16">Heb. xi. 16</reference>), is a key to this argument, where, when he had been speaking of the faith and obedience of the patriarchs in the land of their pilgrimage, he adds, <hi type="italic">Wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God;</hi> because <hi type="italic">he has provided for them a city,</hi> a heavenly city; implying, that if he had not provided so well for them in the other world, considering how they sped in this, he would have been ashamed to have called himself <hi type="italic">their God;</hi> but now he is not, having done that for them which answers it in its true intent and full extent. <div eID="gen23369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23370" type="x-p"/> (2.) That the soul is immortal, and the body shall rise again, to be united; if the former point be gained, these will follow; but they are likewise proved by considering the time when God spoke this; it was to Moses at the bush, long after Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, were dead and buried; and yet God saith, not, "<hi type="italic">I was,</hi>" or "<hi type="italic">have been,</hi>" but <hi type="italic">I am the God of Abraham.</hi> Now <hi type="italic">God is not God of the dead, but of the living.</hi> He is a living God, and communicates vital influences to those to whom he is a God. If, when Abraham died, there had been an end of him, there had been an end likewise of God's relation to him as his God; but at that time, when God spoke to Moses, he was the God of Abraham, and therefore Abraham must be then alive; which proves the immortality of the soul in a state of bliss; and that, by consequence, infers the resurrection of the body; for there is such an inclination in the human soul to its body, as would make a final and eternal separation inconsistent with the bliss of those that have God for <hi type="italic">their God.</hi> The Sadducees' notion was, that the union between body and soul is so close, that, when the body dies, the soul dies with it. Now, upon the same hypothesis, if the soul lives, as it certainly does, the body must some time or other live with it. And besides, the Lord is for the body, it is an essential part of the man; there is a covenant with the dust, which will be remembered, otherwise <hi type="italic">the man</hi> would not be happy. The charge which the dying patriarchs gave concerning their bones, and that <hi type="italic">in faith,</hi> was an evidence that they had some expectation of the resurrection of their bodies. But this doctrine was reserved for a more full revelation after the resurrection of Christ, who <hi type="italic">was the first-fruits of them that slept.</hi> <div eID="gen23370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23371" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> We have the issue of this dispute. The Sadducees were <hi type="italic">put to silence</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.34">v. 34</reference>), and so put to shame. They thought by their subtlety to put Christ to shame, when they were preparing shame for themselves. But the multitude <hi type="italic">were astonished at this doctrine,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.22.33">v. 33</reference>. 1. Because it was new to them. See to what a sad pass the exposition of scripture was come among them, when people were astonished at it as a miracle to hear the fundamental promise applied to this great truth; they had sorry scribes, or this had been no news to them. 2. Because it had something in it very good and great. Truth often shows the brighter, and is the more admired, for its being opposed. Observe, Many gainsayers are silenced, and many hearers astonished, without being savingly converted; yet even in the silence and astonishment of unsanctified souls God magnifies his law, magnifies his gospel, and makes both honourable.
entries.dc3fa7f30082766c329e793e1299077d64e6edad: <div eID="gen23371" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Substance of the Commandments.</title> <div sID="gen23372" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">34</hi> But when the Pharisees had heard that he had put the Sadducees to silence, they were gathered together. <hi type="super">35</hi> Then one of them, <hi type="italic">which was</hi> a lawyer, asked <hi type="italic">him a question,</hi> tempting him, and saying, <hi type="super">36</hi> Master, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> the great commandment in the law? <hi type="super">37</hi> Jesus said unto him, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. <hi type="super">38</hi> This is the first and great commandment. <hi type="super">39</hi> And the second <hi type="italic">is</hi> like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. <hi type="super">40</hi> On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets. <div eID="gen23372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23373" type="x-p"/> Here is a discourse which Christ had with a Pharisee-lawyer, about the great commandment of the law. Observe, <div eID="gen23373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23374" type="x-p"/> I. The combination of the Pharisees against Christ, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.34">v. 34</reference>. They heard <hi type="italic">that he had put the Sadducees to silence,</hi> had stopped their mouths, though their understandings were not opened; and they were <hi type="italic">gathered together,</hi> not to return him the thanks of their party, as they ought to have done, for his effectually asserting and confirming of the truth against the Sadducees, the common enemies of their religion, but to <hi type="italic">tempt him,</hi> in hopes to get the reputation of puzzling him who had puzzled the Sadducees. They were more vexed that Christ was honoured, than pleased that the Sadducees were silenced; being more concerned for their own tyranny and traditions, which Christ opposed, than for the doctrine of the resurrection and a future state, which the Sadducees opposed. Note, It is an instance of Pharisaical envy and malice, to be displeased at the maintaining of a confessed truth, when it is done by those we do not like; to sacrifice a public good to private piques and prejudices. Blessed Paul was otherwise minded, <reference osisRef="Phil.1.18">Phil. i. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen23374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23375" type="x-p"/> II. The lawyer's question, which he put to Christ. The lawyers were students in, and teachers of, the law of Moses, as the scribes were; but some think that in <hi type="italic">this</hi> they differed, that they dealt more in practical questions than the scribes; they studied and professed casuistical divinity. This lawyer <hi type="italic">asked him a question, tempting him;</hi> not with any design to ensnare him, as appears by St. Mark's relation of the story, where we find that this was he to whom Christ said, <hi type="italic">Thou are not far from the kingdom of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.12.34">Mark xii. 34</reference>, but only to see what he would say, and to draw on discourse with him, to satisfy his own and his friends' curiosity. <div eID="gen23375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23376" type="x-p"/> 1. The question was, <hi type="italic">Master, which is the greatest commandment of the law?</hi> A needless question, when all the things of God's law are great things (<reference osisRef="Hos.8.12">Hos. viii. 12</reference>), and the wisdom from above is without partiality, partiality in the law (<reference osisRef="Mal.2.9">Mal. ii. 9</reference>), and hath respect to them all. Yet it is true, there are some commands that are the principles of the oracles of God, more extensive and inclusive than others. Our Saviour speaks of the <hi type="italic">weightier matters of the law,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.23.23">ch. xxiii. 23</reference>. <div eID="gen23376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23377" type="x-p"/> 2. The design was to try him, or tempt him; to try, not so much his knowledge as his judgment. It was a question disputed among the critics in the law. Some would have the law of circumcision to be the great commandment, others the law of the sabbath, others the law of sacrifices, according as they severally stood affected, and spent their zeal; now they would try what Christ said to this question, hoping to incense the people against him, if he should not answer according to the vulgar opinion; and if he should magnify one commandment, they would reflect on him as vilifying the rest. The question was harmless enough; and it appears by comparing <reference osisRef="Luke.10.27-Luke.10.28">Luke x. 27, 28</reference>, that it was an adjudged point among the lawyers, that the <hi type="italic">love of God</hi> and our <hi type="italic">neighbour</hi> is the great commandment, and the sum of all the rest, and Christ had there approved it; so the putting of it to him here seems rather a scornful design to catechise him as a child, than spiteful design to dispute with him as an adversary. <div eID="gen23377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23378" type="x-p"/> III. Christ's answer to this question; it is well for us that such a question was asked him, that we might have his answer. It is no disparagement to great men to answer plain questions. Now Christ recommends to us those as the great commandments, not which are so exclusive of others, but which are <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> great because inclusive of others. Observe, <div eID="gen23378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23379" type="x-p"/> 1. Which these great commandments are (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.37-Matt.22.39">v. 37-39</reference>); not the judicial laws, those could not be the greatest now that the people of the Jews, to whom they pertained, were so little; not the ceremonial laws, those could not be the greatest, now that they were waxen old, and were ready to vanish away; nor any particular moral precept; but the love of God and our neighbour, which are the spring and foundation of all the rest, which (these being supposed) will follow of course. <div eID="gen23379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23380" type="x-p"/> (1.) All the law is fulfilled in one word, and that is, <hi type="italic">love.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Rom.13.10">Rom. xiii. 10</reference>. All obedience begins in the affections, and nothing in religion is done right, that is not done there first. Love is the leading affection, which gives law, and gives ground, to the rest; and therefore that, as the main fort, is to be first secured and garrisoned for God. Man is a creature cut out for love; thus therefore is the law written in the heart, that it is a <hi type="italic">law of love.</hi> Love is a short and sweet word; and, if that be <hi type="italic">the fulfilling of the law,</hi> surely the yoke of the command is very easy. Love is the rest and satisfaction of the soul; if we walk in this good old way, we shall find rest. <div eID="gen23380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23381" type="x-p"/> (2.) The <hi type="italic">love of God</hi> is the first and great commandment of all, and the summary of all the commands of the first table. The proper act of love being complacency, good is the proper object of it. Now God, being good infinitely, originally, and eternally, is to be loved in the first place, and nothing loved beside him, but what is loved for him. <hi type="italic">Love</hi> is the first and great thing that God demands from us, and therefore the first and great thing that we should devote to him. <div eID="gen23381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23382" type="x-p"/> Now here we are directed, <div eID="gen23382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23383" type="x-p"/> [1.] To love God as ours; <hi type="italic">Thou shalt love the Lord thy God</hi> as thine. The first commandment is, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt have no other God;</hi> which implies that we must have him for our God, and that will engage our love to him. Those that made the sun and moon their gods, loved them, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.2">Jer. viii. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.18.24">Judges xviii. 24</reference>. To love God as ours is to love him because he is ours, our Creator, Owner, and Ruler, and to conduct ourselves to him as ours, with obedience to him, and dependence on him. We must love God as reconciled to us, and made ours by covenant; that is the foundation of this, <hi type="italic">Thy God.</hi> <div eID="gen23383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23384" type="x-p"/> [2.] To love him <hi type="italic">with all our heart, and soul, and mind.</hi> Some make these to signify one and the same thing, to love him with all our powers; others distinguish them; the heart, soul, and mind, are the will, affections, and understanding; or the vital, sensitive, and intellectual faculties. Our love of God must be a sincere love, and not in word and tongue only, as theirs is who say they love him, but their hearts are not with him. It must be a strong love, we must love him in the most intense degree; as we must <hi type="italic">praise</hi> him, so we must <hi type="italic">love</hi> him, with <hi type="italic">all that is within us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.103.1">Ps. ciii. 1</reference>. It must be a singular and superlative love, we must love him more than any thing else; this way the stream of our affections must entirely run. The heart must be united to love God, in opposition to a divided heart. All our love is too little to bestow upon him, and therefore all the powers of the soul must be engaged for him, and carried out toward him. <hi type="italic">This is the first and great commandment;</hi> for obedience to this is the spring of obedience to all the rest; which is <hi type="italic">then</hi> only acceptable, when it flows from love. <div eID="gen23384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23385" type="x-p"/> (3.) To <hi type="italic">love our neighbour as ourselves</hi> is the <hi type="italic">second</hi> great commandment (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.39">v. 39</reference>); <hi type="italic">It is like unto that first;</hi> it is inclusive of all the precepts of the second table, as that is of the first. It is <hi type="italic">like</hi> it, for it is founded upon it, and flows from it; and a right love to our brother, whom we have seen, is both an instance and an evidence of our <hi type="italic">love to God, whom we have not seen,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.20">1 John iv. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen23385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23386" type="x-p"/> [1.] It is implied, that we do, and should, love ourselves. There is a self-love which is corrupt, and the root of the greatest sins, and it must be put off and mortified: but there is a self-love which is natural, and the rule of the greatest duty, and it must be preserved and sanctified. We must love ourselves, that is, we must have a due regard to the dignity of our own natures, and a due concern for the welfare of our own souls and bodies. <div eID="gen23386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23387" type="x-p"/> [2.] It is prescribed, that we <hi type="italic">love our neighbour as ourselves.</hi> We must honour and esteem all men, and must wrong and injure none; must have a good will to all, and good wishes for all, and, as we have opportunity, must do good to all. We must love our neighbour as ourselves, as truly and sincerely as we love ourselves, and in the same instances; nay, in many cases we must deny ourselves for the good of our neighbour, and must make ourselves servants to the true welfare of others, and be willing to <hi type="italic">spend and be spent for them,</hi> to <hi type="italic">lay down our lives for the brethren.</hi> <div eID="gen23387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23388" type="x-p"/> 2. Observe what the weight and greatness of these commandments is (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.40">v. 40</reference>); <hi type="italic">On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets;</hi> that is, This is the sum and substance of all those precepts relating to practical religion which were written in men's hearts by nature, revived by Moses, and backed and enforced by the preaching and writing of the prophets. All hang upon the law of love; take away this, and all falls to the ground, and comes to nothing. Rituals and ceremonials must give way to these, as must all spiritual gifts, for love is the more excellent way. This is the spirit of the law, which animates it, the cement of the law, which joins it; it is the root and spring of all other duties, the compendium of the whole Bible, not only of the law and the prophets, but of the gospel too, only supposing this love to be the fruit of faith, and that we love God in Christ, and our neighbour for his sake. All hangs on these two commandments, as the effect doth both on its efficient and on its final cause; for <hi type="italic">the fulfilling of the law is love</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.13.10">Rom. xiii. 10</reference>) and <hi type="italic">the end of the law is love,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.5">1 Tim. i. 5</reference>. The law of love is the nail, is the <hi type="italic">nail in the sure place, fastened by the masters of assemblies</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.12.11">Eccl. xii. 11</reference>), on which is hung all <hi type="italic">the glory of the law and the prophets</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.24">Isa. xxii. 24</reference>), a nail that shall never be drawn; for on this nail all the glory of the new Jerusalem shall eternally hang. <hi type="italic">Love never faileth.</hi> Into these two great commandments therefore let our hearts be delivered as into a mould; in the defence and evidence of these let us spend our zeal, and not in notions, names, and strifes of words, as if those were the mighty things on which the law and the prophets hung, and to them the love of God and our neighbour must be sacrificed; but to the commanding power of these let every thing else be made to bow.
entries.64c0ee64de7fd64bae6b7066bad76cc085a030ee: <div eID="gen23388" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Pharisees Silenced.</title> <div sID="gen23389" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">41</hi> While the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them, <hi type="super">42</hi> Saying, What think ye of Christ? whose son is he? They say unto him, <hi type="italic">The Son</hi> of David. <hi type="super">43</hi> He saith unto them, How then doth David in spirit call him Lord, saying, <hi type="super">44</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto my Lord, Sit thou on my right hand, till I make thine enemies thy footstool? <hi type="super">45</hi> If David then call him Lord, how is he his son? <hi type="super">46</hi> And no man was able to answer him a word, neither durst any <hi type="italic">man</hi> from that day forth ask him any more <hi type="italic">questions.</hi> <div eID="gen23389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23390" type="x-p"/> Many questions the Pharisees had asked Christ, by which, though they thought to pose him, they did but <hi type="italic">ex</hi>pose themselves; but now let him ask them a question; and he will do it when they are gathered together, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.41">v. 41</reference>. He did not take some one of them apart from the rest (<hi type="italic">ne Hercules contra duos—Hercules himself may be overmatched</hi>), but, to shame them the more, he took them all together, when they were in confederacy and consulting against him, and yet puzzled them. Note, God delights to baffle his enemies when they most strengthen themselves; he gives them all the advantages they can wish for, and yet conquers them. <hi type="italic">Associate yourselves, and you shall be broken in pieces,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.3.9-Isa.3.10">Isa. iii. 9, 10</reference>. Now here, <div eID="gen23390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23391" type="x-p"/> I. Christ proposes a question to them, which they could easily answer; it was a question in their own catechism; "<hi type="italic">What think ye of Christ? Whose Son is He?</hi> Whose Son do you expect the Messiah to be, who was promised to the fathers?" This they could easily answer, <hi type="italic">The Son of David.</hi> It was the common periphrasis of the Messiah; they called him <hi type="italic">the Son of David.</hi> So the scribes, who expounded the scripture, had taught them, from <reference osisRef="Ps.89.35-Ps.89.36">Ps. lxxxix. 35, 36</reference>, <hi type="italic">I will not lie unto David; his seed shall endure for ever</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.7">Isa. ix. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">upon the throne of David.</hi> And <reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">Isa. xi. 1</reference>, <hi type="italic">A rod out of the stem of Jesse.</hi> The covenant of royalty made with David was a figure of the covenant of redemption made with Christ, who as David, was made King <hi type="italic">with an oath,</hi> and was first humbled and then advanced. If Christ was the Son of David, he was really and truly Man. Israel said, <hi type="italic">We have ten parts in David;</hi> and Judah said, <hi type="italic">He is our bone and our flesh;</hi> what part have we then in the Son of David, who took our nature upon him? <div eID="gen23391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23392" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">What think ye of Christ?</hi> They had put questions to him, one after another, out of the law; but he comes and puts a question to them upon the promise. Many are so full of the law, that they forget Christ, as if their duties would save them without his merit and grace. It concerns each of us seriously to ask ourselves, What think we of Christ? Some think not of him at all, he is not in all, not in any, of their thoughts; some think meanly, and some think hardly, of him; but <hi type="italic">to them that believe he is precious;</hi> and <hi type="italic">how precious then are the thoughts of him!</hi> While <hi type="italic">the daughters of Jerusalem</hi> think no more of Christ than of <hi type="italic">another beloved;</hi> the spouse thinks of him as <hi type="italic">the Chief of ten thousands.</hi> <div eID="gen23392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23393" type="x-p"/> II. He starts a difficulty upon their answer, which they could not easily solve, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.43-Matt.22.45">v. 43-45</reference>. Many can so readily affirm the truth, that they think they have knowledge enough to be proud of, who, when they are called to confirm the truth, and to vindicate and defend it, show they have ignorance enough to be ashamed of. The objection Christ raised was, <hi type="italic">If Christ be David's son, how then doth David, in spirit, call him Lord?</hi> He did not hereby design to ensnare them, as they did him, but to instruct them in a truth they were loth to believe—that the expected Messiah is God. <div eID="gen23393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23394" type="x-p"/> 1. It is easy to see that David calls Christ <hi type="italic">Lord,</hi> and this in spirit being divinely inspired, and actuated therein by a spirit of prophecy; for it was <hi type="italic">the Spirit of the Lord that spoke by him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.1-2Sam.23.2">2 Sam. xxiii. 1, 2</reference>. David was one of those <hi type="italic">holy men that spoke as</hi> they were <hi type="italic">moved by the Holy Ghost,</hi> especially in calling Christ <hi type="italic">Lord;</hi> for it was then, as it is still (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.3">1 Cor. xii. 3</reference>) that <hi type="italic">no man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost.</hi> Now, to prove that David, in spirit, called Christ <hi type="italic">Lord,</hi> he quotes <reference osisRef="Ps.110.1">Ps. cx. 1</reference>, which psalm the scribes themselves understood of Christ; of him, it is certain, the prophet there speaks, of him and of no other man; and it is a prophetical summary of the doctrine of Christ, it describes him executing the offices of a Prophet, Priest, and King, both in his humiliation and also in his exaltation. <div eID="gen23394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23395" type="x-p"/> Christ quotes the whole verse, which shows the Redeemer in his exaltation; (1.) <hi type="italic">Sitting at the right hand of God.</hi> His sitting denotes both rest and rule; his sitting at God's right hand denotes superlative honour and sovereign power. See in what great words this is expressed (<reference osisRef="Heb.8.1">Heb. viii. 1</reference>); <hi type="italic">He is set on the right hand of the throne of the Majesty.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Phil.2.9">Phil. ii. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.20">Eph. i. 20</reference>. He did not take this honour to himself, but was entitled to it by covenant with his Father, and invested in it by commission from him, and here is that commission. (2.) Subduing his enemies. There he shall sit, till they be all made either his friends or his footstool. <hi type="italic">The carnal mind,</hi> wherever it is, <hi type="italic">is enmity to Christ;</hi> and that is subdued in the <hi type="italic">conversion of the willing people that are called to his foot</hi> (as the expression is, <reference osisRef="Isa.41.2">Isa. xli. 2</reference>), and in the confusion of his impenitent adversaries, who shall be brought under his foot, as the kings of Canaan were under the feet of Joshua. <div eID="gen23395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23396" type="x-p"/> But that which this verse is quoted for is, that David calls the Messiah <hi type="italic">his Lord; the Lord,</hi> Jehovah, <hi type="italic">said unto my Lord.</hi> This intimates to us, that in expounding scripture we must take notice of, and improve, not only that which is the main scope and sense of a verse, but of the words and phrases, by which they Spirit chooses to express that sense, which have often a very useful and instructive significance. Here is a good note from that word, <hi type="italic">My Lord.</hi> <div eID="gen23396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23397" type="x-p"/> 2. It is not so easy for those who believe not the Godhead of the Messiah, to clear this from an absurdity, if Christ be David's son. It is incongruous for the father to speak of his son, the predecessor of his successor, as his <hi type="italic">Lord.</hi> If David call him <hi type="italic">Lord,</hi> that is laid down (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.45">v. 45</reference>) as the <hi type="italic">magis notum—the more evident truth;</hi> for whatever is said of Christ's humanity and humiliation must be construed and understood in consistency with the truth of his divine nature and dominion. We must hold this fast, that he is David's Lord, and by that explain his being David's son. The seeming differences of scripture, as here, may not only be accommodated, but contribute to the beauty and harmony of the whole. <hi type="italic">Amicæ scripturarum lites, utinam et nostræ—The differences observable in the scriptures are of a friendly kind; would to God that our differences were of the same kind!</hi> <div eID="gen23397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23398" type="x-p"/> III. We have here the success of this gentle trial which Christ made of the Pharisees' knowledge, in two things. <div eID="gen23398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23399" type="x-p"/> 1. It puzzled them (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.46">v. 46</reference>); <hi type="italic">No man was able to answer him a word.</hi> Either it was their ignorance that they did not know, or their impiety that they would not own, the Messiah to be God; which truth was the only key to unlock this difficulty. What those Rabbies could not then answer, blessed be God, the plainest Christian that is led into the understanding of the gospel of Christ, can now account for; that Christ, as God, was David's <hi type="italic">Lord;</hi> and Christ, as Man, was David's <hi type="italic">son.</hi> This he did not now himself explain, but reserved it till the proof of it was completed by his resurrection; but we have it fully explained by him in his glory (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.16">Rev. xxii. 16</reference>); <hi type="italic">I am the root and the offspring of David.</hi> Christ, as God, was David's <hi type="italic">Root;</hi> Christ, as Man, was David's <hi type="italic">Offspring.</hi> If we hold not fast this truth, that Jesus Christ is over all God blessed for ever, we run ourselves into inextricable difficulties. And well might David, his remote ancestor, call him <hi type="italic">Lord,</hi> when Mary, his immediate mother, after she had conceived him, <hi type="italic">called him, Lord and God, her Saviour,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.46-Luke.1.47">Luke i. 46, 47</reference>. <div eID="gen23399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23400" type="x-p"/> 2. It silenced them, and all others that sought occasion against him; <hi type="italic">Neither durst any man, from that day forth, ask him any more</hi> such captious, tempting, ensnaring <hi type="italic">questions.</hi> Note, God will glorify himself in the silencing of many whom he will not glorify himself in the salvation of. Many are convinced, that are not converted, by the word. Had these been converted, they would have asked him more questions, especially that great question, <hi type="italic">What must we do to be saved?</hi> But since they could not gain their point, they would have no more to do with him. But, thus all that strive with their Master shall be convinced, as these Pharisees and lawyers here were, of the inequality of the match.  <chapter eID="Matt.22"/> <div eID="gen23400" type="x-p"/>

entries.aadb89a80d2a843698efe15f7dec1a8ad16b9784: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13743"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 22</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.22.1-Matt.22.14">Mt 22:1-14</reference>. Parable of the Marriage of the King's Son.</title> <div sID="gen26364" type="x-p"/> This is a different parable from that of the Great Supper, in <reference osisRef="Luke.14.15">Lu 14:15</reference>, &c., and is recorded by Matthew alone.<div eID="gen26364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26365" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13743"/><hi type="bold">2. The kingdom of heaven is like unto a certain king, which made a marriage for his son--</hi>"In this parable," as Trench admirably remarks, "we see how the Lord is revealing Himself in ever clearer light as the central Person of the kingdom, giving here a far plainer hint than in the last parable of the nobility of His descent. There He was indeed the Son, the only and beloved one (<reference osisRef="Mark.12.6">Mr 12:6</reference>), of the Householder; but here His race is royal, and He appears as Himself at once the King and the King's Son (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.1">Psa 72:1</reference>). The last was a parable of the Old Testament history; and Christ is rather the last and greatest of the line of its prophets and teachers than the founder of a new kingdom. In that, God appears demanding something from men; in this, a parable of grace, God appears more as giving something to them. Thus, as often, the two complete each other: this taking up the matter where the other left it." The "marriage" of Jehovah to His people Israel was familiar to Jewish ears; and in <reference osisRef="Ps.45.1-Ps.45.17">Psa 45:1-17</reference> this marriage is seen consummated in the Person of Messiah "THE King," Himself addressed as "God" and yet as anointed by "His God" with the oil of gladness above His fellows. These apparent contradictions (see on <reference osisRef="Luke.20.41-Luke.20.44">Lu 20:41-44</reference>) are resolved in this parable; and Jesus, in claiming to be this King's Son, serves Himself Heir to all that the prophets and sweet singers of Israel held forth as to Jehovah's ineffably near and endearing union to His people. But observe carefully, that THE Bride does not come into view in this parable; its design being to teach certain truths under the figure of guests at a wedding feast, and the want of a wedding garment, which would not have harmonized with the introduction of the Bride. <div eID="gen26365" type="x-p"/>
entries.4695396060df60629432f2e9cb6826e816609245: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13744"/><div sID="gen26366" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13744"/><hi type="bold">3. and sent forth his servants--</hi>representing all preachers of the Gospel.<div eID="gen26366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26367" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to call them that were bidden--</hi>here meaning the Jews, who were "bidden," from the first choice of them onwards through every summons addressed to them by the prophets to hold themselves in readiness for the appearing of their King.<div eID="gen26367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26368" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to the wedding--</hi>or the marriage festivities, when the preparations were all concluded.<div eID="gen26368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26369" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and they would not come--</hi>as the issue of the whole ministry of the Baptist, our Lord Himself, and His apostles thereafter, too sadly showed. <div eID="gen26369" type="x-p"/>
entries.48011ffe4ba412a7b6ed83c2358263b10e60d36c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13745"/><div sID="gen26370" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13745"/><hi type="bold">4. my oxen and my fatlings are killed, and all things are ready; come unto the marriage--</hi>This points to those Gospel calls after Christ's death, resurrection, ascension, and effusion of the Spirit, to which the parable could not directly allude, but when only it could be said, with strict propriety, "that all things were ready." Compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.7">1Co 5:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.8">8</reference>, "Christ our Passover is sacrificed for us; therefore, let us keep the feast"; also <reference osisRef="John.6.51">Joh 6:51</reference>, "I am the living bread which came down from heaven: if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever: and the bread which I will give is My flesh, which I will give for the life of the world." <div eID="gen26370" type="x-p"/>
entries.d40f46a05df0854c64df7e58e7b093110cde0d2d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13746"/><div sID="gen26371" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13746"/>5. But they made light of it, and went their ways, one to his farm, another to his merchandise: <div eID="gen26371" type="x-p"/>
entries.d5cbb7d85a19a5b830b935f98d5873a7fa8a8eba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13747"/><div sID="gen26372" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13747"/><hi type="bold">6. And the remnant took his servants, and entreated them spitefully--</hi>insulted them.<div eID="gen26372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26373" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and slew them--</hi>These are two different classes of unbelievers: the one simply indifferent; the other absolutely hostile--the one, contemptuous scorners; the other, bitter persecutors. <div eID="gen26373" type="x-p"/>
entries.ac6cee6b562b517cc88c29bcf662e338f8b4fd6d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13748"/><div sID="gen26374" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13748"/><hi type="bold">7. But when the king--</hi>the Great God, who is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.<div eID="gen26374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26375" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heard thereof, he was wroth--</hi>at the affront put both on His Son, and on Himself who had deigned to invite them.<div eID="gen26375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26376" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and he sent forth his armies--</hi>The Romans are here styled God's armies, just as the Assyrian is styled "the rod of His anger" (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.5">Is 10:5</reference>), as being the executors of His judicial vengeance.<div eID="gen26376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26377" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and destroyed those murderers--</hi>and in what vast numbers did they do it!<div eID="gen26377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26378" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and burned up their city--</hi>Ah! Jerusalem, once "the city of the Great King" (<reference osisRef="Ps.48.2">Psa 48:2</reference>), and even up almost to this time (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.35">Mt 5:35</reference>); but now it is "their city"--just as our Lord, a day or two after this, said of the temple, where God had so long dwelt, "Behold your house is left unto you desolate" (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.38">Mt 23:38</reference>)! Compare <reference osisRef="Luke.19.43">Lu 19:43</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.19.44">44</reference>. <div eID="gen26378" type="x-p"/>
entries.10ea159bdc10195b988791834a75be1d78992fea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13749"/><div sID="gen26379" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13749"/><hi type="bold">8. The wedding is ready, but they which were bidden were not worthy--</hi>for how should those be deemed worthy to sit down at His table who had affronted Him by their treatment of His gracious invitation? <div eID="gen26379" type="x-p"/>
entries.02490f818b66a52091ebbfed6ba96c0c6f0f69ab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13750"/><div sID="gen26380" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13750"/><hi type="bold">9. Go ye therefore into the highways--</hi>the great outlets and thoroughfares, whether of town or country, where human beings are to be found.<div eID="gen26380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26381" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and as many as ye shall find, bid to the marriage--</hi>that is, just as they are. <div eID="gen26381" type="x-p"/>
entries.83977b531c84246b4ee20af802e2d61625cdc960: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13751"/><div sID="gen26382" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13751"/><hi type="bold">10. So those servants went out into the highways, and gathered together all as many as they found, both bad and good--</hi>that is, without making any distinction between open sinners and the morally correct. The Gospel call fetched in Jews, Samaritans, and outlying heathen alike. Thus far the parable answers to that of "the Great Supper" (<reference osisRef="Luke.14.16">Lu 14:16</reference>, &c.). But the distinguishing feature of our parable is what follows: <div eID="gen26382" type="x-p"/>
entries.33e81a70b277d0f3fbc05769a8536e952047d69f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13752"/><div sID="gen26383" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13752"/><hi type="bold">11. And when the king came in to see the guests--</hi>Solemn expression this, of that omniscient inspection of every professed disciple of the Lord Jesus from age to age, in virtue of which his true character will hereafter be judicially proclaimed!<div eID="gen26383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26384" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he saw there a man--</hi>This shows that it is the judgment of individuals which is intended in this latter part of the parable: the first part represents rather national judgment.<div eID="gen26384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26385" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which had not on a wedding garment--</hi>The language here is drawn from the following remarkable passage in <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.7">Zep 1:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.8">8</reference>:--"Hold thy peace at the presence of the Lord God; for the day of the Lord is at hand: for the Lord hath prepared a sacrifice, He hath bid His guests. And it shall come to pass in the day of the Lord's sacrifice, that I will punish the princes, and the king's children, and all such as are clothed with strange apparel." The custom in the East of presenting festival garments (see <reference osisRef="Gen.45.22">Ge 45:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.22">2Ki 5:22</reference>), even though nor clearly proved, Is certainly presupposed here. It undoubtedly means something which they bring not of their own--for how could they have any such dress who were gathered in from the highways indiscriminately?--but which they receive as their appropriate dress. And what can that be but what is meant by "putting on the Lord Jesus," as "The Lord Our Righteousness?" (See <reference osisRef="Ps.45.13">Psa 45:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.14">14</reference>). Nor could such language be strange to those in whose ears had so long resounded those words of prophetic joy: "I will greatly rejoice in the Lord, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for He hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, He hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels" (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.10">Is 61:10</reference>). <div eID="gen26385" type="x-p"/>
entries.e20e90f117fb568af5f8f8a24e9f40b0f61f7b36: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13753"/><div sID="gen26386" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13753"/>12. Friend, how camest thou in hither, not having a wedding garment? <hi type="bold">And he was speechless--</hi>being self-condemned. <div eID="gen26386" type="x-p"/>
entries.af0f5d98847ff665535bf8ff922d42fb18489f45: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13754"/><div sID="gen26387" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13754"/><hi type="bold">13. Then said the king to the servants--</hi>the angelic ministers of divine vengeance (as in <reference osisRef="Matt.13.41">Mt 13:41</reference>).<div eID="gen26387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26388" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Bind him hand and foot--</hi>putting it out of his power to resist.<div eID="gen26388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26389" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and take him away, and cast him into outer darkness--</hi>So <reference osisRef="Matt.8.12">Mt 8:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.25.30">25:30</reference>. The expression is emphatic--"the darkness which is outside." To be "outside" at all--or, in the language of <reference osisRef="Rev.22.15">Re 22:15</reference>, to be "without" the heavenly city, excluded from its joyous nuptials and gladsome festivities--is sad enough of itself, without anything else. But to find themselves not only excluded from the brightness and glory and joy and felicity of the kingdom above, but thrust into a region of "darkness," with all its horrors, this is the dismal retribution here announced, that awaits the unworthy at the great day.<div eID="gen26389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26390" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there--</hi>in that region and condition.<div eID="gen26390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26391" type="x-p"/> shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth. See on <reference osisRef="Matt.13.42">Mt 13:42</reference>. <div eID="gen26391" type="x-p"/>
entries.11b6191270bbee19f2270272dc4b08bdf33fb2e0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13755"/><div sID="gen26392" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13755"/><hi type="bold">14. For many are called, but few are chosen--</hi>So <reference osisRef="Matt.19.30">Mt 19:30</reference>. See on <reference osisRef="Matt.20.16">Mt 20:16</reference>.<div eID="gen26392" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.22.15-Matt.22.40">Mt 22:15-40</reference>. Entangling Questions about Tribute, the Resurrection, and the Great Commandment, with the Replies. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.12.13-Mark.12.34">Mr 12:13-34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.20.20-Luke.20.40">Lu 20:20-40</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen26393" type="x-p"/> For the exposition, see on <reference osisRef="Mark.12.13-Mark.12.34">Mr 12:13-34</reference>.<div eID="gen26393" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.22.41-Matt.22.46">Mt 22:41-46</reference>. Christ Baffles the Pharisees by a Question about David and Messiah. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.12.35-Mark.12.37">Mr 12:35-37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.20.41-Luke.20.44">Lu 20:41-44</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen26394" type="x-p"/> For the exposition, see on <reference osisRef="Mark.12.35-Mark.12.37">Mr 12:35-37</reference>.  <chapter eID="Matt.22"/>

entries.4d7eb519e15e0fadfd6613ec3020011bb482cf1a: <div eID="gen38108" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen38109" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen38110" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen38110" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen38109" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen38111" type="x-p"/> The parable of the marriage of a king's son, <reference osisRef="Mat.22.1-Mat.22.14">Mat 22:1-14</reference>. The Pharisees and Herodians question him concerning the lawfulness of paying tribute to Caesar, <reference osisRef="Mat.22.15-Mat.22.22">Mat 22:15-22</reference>. The Sadducees question him concerning the resurrection, <reference osisRef="Mat.22.23-Mat.22.33">Mat 22:23-33</reference>. A lawyer questions him concerning the greatest commandment in the law, <reference osisRef="Mat.22.34-Mat.22.40">Mat 22:34-40</reference>. He asks them their opinion of the Christ, and confounds them, <reference osisRef="Mat.22.41-Mat.22.46">Mat 22:41-46</reference>.
entries.13982e6f46bb0ad67b7603e9c2fc854faf32298c: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen38111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38112" type="x-p"/> The kingdom of heaven - In Bereshith Rabba, sect. 62. fol. 60, there is a parable very similar to this, and another still more so in Sohar. Levit. fol. 40. But these rabbinical parables are vastly ennobled by passing through the hands of our Lord. It appears from Luke, <reference osisRef="Luk.14.15">Luk 14:15</reference>; etc., that it was at an entertainment that this parable was originally spoken. It was a constant practice of our Lord to take the subjects of his discourses from the persons present, or from the circumstances of times, persons, and places. See <reference osisRef="Mat.16.6">Mat 16:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joh.4.7-Joh.4.10">Joh 4:7-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joh.6.26">Joh 6:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.6.27">Joh 6:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joh.7.37">Joh 7:37</reference>. A preacher that can do so can never be at a loss for text or sermon. <div eID="gen38112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38113" type="x-p"/> A marriage for his son - A marriage feast, so the word γαμους properly means. Or a feast of inauguration, when his son was put in possession of the government, and thus he and his new subjects became married together. See <reference osisRef="1Kgs.1.5-1Kgs.1.9">1Kgs 1:5-9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.1.19">1Kgs 1:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.1.25">1Kgs 1:25</reference>, etc., where such a feast is mentioned. <div eID="gen38113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38114" type="x-p"/> From this parable it appears plain, <div eID="gen38114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38115" type="x-p"/> 1. That the King means the great God. <div eID="gen38115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38116" type="x-p"/> 2. His Son, the Lord Jesus. <div eID="gen38116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38117" type="x-p"/> 3. The Marriage, his incarnation, or espousing human nature, by taking it into union with himself. <div eID="gen38117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38118" type="x-p"/> 4. The Marriage Feast, the economy of the Gospel, during which men are invited to partake of the blessings purchased by, and consequent on, the incarnation and death of our blessed Lord. <div eID="gen38118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38119" type="x-p"/> 5. By those who Had Been bidden, or invited, <reference osisRef="Mat.22.3">Mat 22:3</reference>, are meant the Jews in general, who had this union of Christ with human nature, and his sacrifice for sin, pointed out by various rites, ceremonies, and sacrifices under the law; and who, by all the prophets, had been constantly invited to believe in and receive the promised Messiah. <div eID="gen38119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38120" type="x-p"/> 6. By the Servants, we are to understand the first preachers of the Gospel, proclaiming salvation to the Jews. John the Baptist and the seventy disciples (<reference osisRef="Luk.10.1">Luk 10:1</reference>), may be here particularly intended. <div eID="gen38120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38121" type="x-p"/> 7. By the Other Servants, <reference osisRef="Mat.22.4">Mat 22:4</reference>, the apostles seem to be meant, who, though they were to preach the Gospel to the whole world, yet were to begin at Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Luk.24.47">Luk 24:47</reference>) with the first offers of mercy. <div eID="gen38121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38122" type="x-p"/> 8. By their making light of it, etc., <reference osisRef="Mat.22.5">Mat 22:5</reference>, is pointed out their neglect of this salvation, and their preferring secular enjoyments, etc., to the kingdom of Christ. <div eID="gen38122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38123" type="x-p"/> 9. By injuriously using some, and slaying others, of his servants, <reference osisRef="Mat.22.6">Mat 22:6</reference>, is pointed out the persecution raised against the apostles by the Jews, in which some of them were martyred. <div eID="gen38123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38124" type="x-p"/> 10. By sending forth his troops, <reference osisRef="Mat.22.7">Mat 22:7</reference>, is meant the commission given to the Romans against Judea; and, burning up their city, the total destruction of Jerusalem by Titus, the son of Vespasian, which happened about forty-one years after. <div eID="gen38124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38125" type="x-p"/> On this parable it is necessary to remark, <div eID="gen38125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38126" type="x-p"/> 1. That man was made at first in union with God. <div eID="gen38126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38127" type="x-p"/> 2. That sin entered in, and separated between God and man. <div eID="gen38127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38128" type="x-p"/> 3. That as there can be no holiness but in union with God, and no heaven without holiness, therefore he provided a way to reconcile and reunite man to himself. <div eID="gen38128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38129" type="x-p"/> 4. This was effected by Christ's uniting himself to human nature, and giving his Spirit to those who believe. <div eID="gen38129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38130" type="x-p"/> 5. That as the marriage union is the closest, the most intimate, solemn, and excellent, of all the connections formed among mortals, and that they who are thus united in the Lord are one flesh; so that mystical union which is formed between God and the soul through Jesus Christ, by the Eternal Spirit, is the closest, most intimate, solemn, and excellent, that can be conceived; for he who is thus joined unto the Lord is one spirit. <div eID="gen38130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38131" type="x-p"/> 6. This contract is made freely: no man can be forced to it, for it is a union of will to will, heart to heart; and it is by willing and consenting that we come unto God through his Son. <div eID="gen38131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38132" type="x-p"/> 7. That if this marriage do not take place here, an eternal separation from God, and from the glory of his power, shall be the fearful consequence. <div eID="gen38132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38133" type="x-p"/> 8. That there are three states in which men run the risk of living without God and losing their souls. 1st. That of a soft, idle, voluptuous life, wherein a man thinks of nothing but quietly to enjoy life, conveniences, riches, private pleasures, and public diversions. They made light of it. 2dly. That of a man wholly taken up with agricultural or commercial employments, in which the love of riches, and application to the means of acquiring them, generally stifle all thoughts of salvation. One went to his own field, and another to his traffic. 3dly. That of a man who is openly unjust, violent, and outrageously wicked, who is a sinner by profession, and not only neglects his salvation, but injuriously treats all those who bring him the Gospel of reconciliation. Seizing his servants, they treated them injuriously, etc.
entries.6f5108c5395b9e5e741b499ace16005e83631e71: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen38133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38134" type="x-p"/> Fatlings - Τα σιτιϚα Properly, fatted rams, or wethers. <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.13">2Sam 6:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.26">1Chr 15:26</reference>.
entries.247b3df0976be3f307442e57728b347c2c6c4210: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen38134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38135" type="x-p"/> But when the king - Himself or, this very king. I have added εκεινος on the authority of nine of the most ancient MSS. and nearly one hundred others; the later Syriac, six copies of the Itala, and some of the fathers. Several printed editions have it, and Griesbach has received it into the text.
entries.453ede33c18560e876c97cb6995174b27b765e16: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen38135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38136" type="x-p"/> Were not worthy - Because they made light of it, and would not come; preferring earthly things to heavenly blessings. Among the Mohammedans, refusal to come to a marriage feast, when invited, is considered a breach of the law of God. Hedayah, vol. iv. p. 91. Any one that shall be invited to a dinner, and does not accept the invitation, disobeys God, and his messenger: and any one who comes uninvited, you may say is a thief, and returns a plunderer. - Mischat ul Mesabih. It was probably considered in this light among all the oriental nations. This observation is necessary, in order to point out more forcibly the iniquity of the refusal mentioned in the text. A man may be said to be worthy of, or fit for, this marriage feast, when, feeling his wretchedness and misery, he comes to God in the way appointed, to get an entrance into the holiest, by the blood of Jesus.
entries.7964a90ec16dab789f2bdc77725b2f5e4c2769f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen38136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38137" type="x-p"/> Go ye therefore into the highways - Διεξοδους των οδων, cross or by-paths; the places where two or more roads met in one, leading into the city, where people were coming together from various quarters of the country. St. Luke adds hedges, to point out the people to whom the apostles were sent, as either miserable vagabonds, or the most indigent poor, who were wandering about the country, or sitting by the sides of the ways and hedges, imploring relief. This verse points out the final rejection of the Jews, and the calling of the Gentiles. It was a custom among the Jews, when a rich man made a feast, to go out and invite in all destitute travelers. See in Rab. Beracoth, fol. 43. <div eID="gen38137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38138" type="x-p"/> As many as ye shall find, bid to the marriage - God sends his salvation to every soul, that all may believe and be saved.
entries.2d0326b05771ba1c80a74c096b6dec8b87fb5647: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen38138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38139" type="x-p"/> Gathered together all - both bad and good - By the preaching of the Gospel, multitudes of souls are gathered into what is generally termed the visible Church of Christ. <div eID="gen38139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38140" type="x-p"/> This Church is the Floor, where the wheat and the chaff are often mingled, <reference osisRef="Mat.3.12">Mat 3:12</reference>. <div eID="gen38140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38141" type="x-p"/> The Field, where the bastard wheat and the true grain grow together, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.26">Mat 13:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.27">Mat 13:27</reference>. <div eID="gen38141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38142" type="x-p"/> The Net, which collects of all kinds, both good and bad, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.48">Mat 13:48</reference>. <div eID="gen38142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38143" type="x-p"/> The House in which the wise and foolish are found, <reference osisRef="Mat.25.1">Mat 25:1</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen38143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38144" type="x-p"/> And the Fold, in which there are both sheep and goats, <reference osisRef="Mat.25.33">Mat 25:33</reference>; etc.
entries.7536cab876b73c8f7d860e56e8437a501bd18456: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen38144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38145" type="x-p"/> When the king came - When God shall come to judge the world. <div eID="gen38145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38146" type="x-p"/> Wedding garment - Among the orientals, long white robes were worn at public festivals; and those who appeared on such occasions with any other garments were esteemed, not only highly culpable, but worthy of punishment. Our Lord seems here to allude to <reference osisRef="Zep.1.7">Zep 1:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zep.1.8">Zep 1:8</reference>, The Lord hath prepared a Sacrifice, he hath Bidden his guests. And it shall come to pass, in the day of the Lord's sacrifice, that I will Punish the princes, and the King's Children, and All Such as are clothed with Strange Apparel. The person who invited the guests prepared such a garment for each, for the time being; and with which he was furnished on his application to the ruler of the feast. It was this which made the conduct of the person mentioned in the text inexcusable; he might have had a proper marriage garment, if he had applied for it. <div eID="gen38146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38147" type="x-p"/> To afford accidental guests clothing suitable to a marriage feast, was a custom among the ancient Greeks. Homer relates that Telemachus, and the son of Nestor, arriving at Lacedaemon when Menelaus was making a marriage feast for his son and daughter, were accommodated with garments suited to the occasion, after having been bathed and anointed. Τους δ' επει ουν δρωμαι λουσαν και χρισαν ελαιῳ, Αμφι δ' αρα χλαινας ουλας βαλον ηδε χιτωνας, Ες ρα θρονους εζοντο παρ' Ατρειδην Μενελαον <div eID="gen38147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38148" type="x-p"/> Odyss. l. iv. ver. 49-51 <div eID="gen38148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38149" type="x-p"/> They entered each a bath, and by the hands <div eID="gen38149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38150" type="x-p"/> Of maidens laved, and oiled, and clothed again <div eID="gen38150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38151" type="x-p"/> With shaggy mantles and resplendent vests, <div eID="gen38151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38152" type="x-p"/> Sat both enthroned at Menelaus' side. <div eID="gen38152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38153" type="x-p"/> Cowper <div eID="gen38153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38154" type="x-p"/> Among the Asiatics, garments called caftans, great numbers of which each nobleman has ordinarily ready in his wardrobe, are given to persons whom he wishes to honor: to refuse to accept or wear such a dress would be deemed the highest insult. <div eID="gen38154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38155" type="x-p"/> This marriage feast or dinner (the communication of the graces of the Gospel in this life) prepares for the marriage supper of the Lamb, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.7-Rev.19.9">Rev 19:7-9</reference>, the enjoyment of eternal blessedness in the kingdom of glory. Now, as without holiness no man can see the Lord, we may at once perceive what our Lord means by the marriage garment - it is Holiness of heart and life: the text last quoted asserts that the fine, white, and clean linen (alluding to the marriage garment above mentioned) was an emblem of the Righteousness of the Saints. Mark this expression: the righteousness, the whole external conduct; regulated according to the will and word of God. Of the Saints, the holy persons, whose souls were purified by the blood of the Lamb.
entries.febf2632d522ad8006c45ddc4494342314d9788f: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen38155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38156" type="x-p"/> He saith unto him, Friend - Rather, companion: so εταιρε should be translated. As this man represents the state of a person in the visible Church, who neglects to come unto the master of the feast for a marriage garment, for the salvation which Christ has procured, he cannot be with any propriety called a friend, but may well be termed a companion, as being a member of the visible Church, and present at all those ordinances where Christ's presence and blessing are found, by all those who sincerely wait upon him for salvation. <div eID="gen38156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38157" type="x-p"/> How camest thou in hither - Why profess to be called by my name while living without a preparation for my kingdom? <div eID="gen38157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38158" type="x-p"/> He was speechless - Εφιμωθη, he was muzzled, or gagged. He had nothing to say in vindication of his neglect. There was a garment provided, but he neither put it on, nor applied for it. His conduct, therefore, was in the highest degree insulting and indecorous. As this man is the emblem, by general consent, of those who shall perish in the last day, may we not ask, without offense, Where does the doctrine of absolute reprobation or preterition appear in his case? If Christ had never died for him, or if he had applied for the garment, and was refused, might he not well have alleged this in behalf of his soul? - and would not the just God have listened to it? But there is not the smallest excuse for him: Christ died, the sacrifice was offered, for him; the ministers of the Gospel invited him; the Holy Spirit strove with him; he might have been saved, but he was not: and the fault lies so absolutely at his own door that the just God is vindicated in his conduct, while he sends him to hell, not for the lack of what he could not get, but for the lack of what he might have had, but either neglected or refused it. <div eID="gen38158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38159" type="x-p"/> Then said the king to the servants - To the ministering angels, executors of the Divine will. <div eID="gen38159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38160" type="x-p"/> Cast him into outer darkness - The Jewish marriages were performed in the night season, and the hall where the feast was made was superbly illuminated; the outer darkness means, therefore, the darkness on the outside of this festal hall; rendered still more gloomy to the person who was suddenly thrust out into it from such a profusion of light. See all this largely treated of on <reference osisRef="Mat.8.12">Mat 8:12</reference> (note).
entries.68e14382b27b04e969838c8c0bb7196030725aed: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen38160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38161" type="x-p"/> Many are called, etc. - This verse is wanting in one of Colbert's MSS., marked 33 in Griesbach. See the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.20.16">Mat 20:16</reference>. Many are called by the preaching of the Gospel into the outward communion of the Church of Christ; but few, comparatively, are chosen to dwell with God in glory, because they do not come to the master of the feast for a marriage garment - for that holiness without which none can see the Lord. This is an allusion to the Roman custom of raising their militia; all were mustered, but only those were chosen to serve, who were found proper. See the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.20.16">Mat 20:16</reference>. Reader! examine thy soul, and make sure work for eternity!
entries.d5c818c8449d5492b5acb752e60aafad5c9f11b0: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen38161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38162" type="x-p"/> In his talk - Εν λογῳ, by discourse: intending to ask him subtle and ensnaring questions; his answers to which might involve him either with the Roman government, or with the great Sanhedrin.
entries.5f4635508a5898212850be25ce307559f4978f14: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen38162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38163" type="x-p"/> The Herodians - For an account of this sect, see the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.16.1">Mat 16:1</reference>. The preceding parable had covered the Pharisees with confusion: when it was ended they went out, not to humble themselves before God, and deprecate the judgments with which they were threatened; but to plot afresh the destruction of their teacher. The depth of their malice appears, <div eID="gen38163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38164" type="x-p"/> 1. In their mode of attack. They had often questioned our Lord on matters concerning religion; and his answers only served to increase his reputation, and their confusion. They now shift their ground, and question him concerning state affairs, and the question is such as must be answered; and yet the answer, to all human appearance, can be none other than what may be construed into a crime against the people, or against the Roman government. <div eID="gen38164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38165" type="x-p"/> 2. Their profound malice appears farther in the choice of their companions in this business, viz. the Herodians. Herod was at this very time at Jerusalem, whither he had come to hold the passover. Jesus, being of Nazareth, which was in Herod's jurisdiction, was considered as his subject. Herod himself was extremely attached to the Roman emperor, and made a public profession of it: all these considerations engaged the Pharisees to unite the Herodians, who, as the Syriac intimates, were the domestics of Herod, in this infernal plot. <div eID="gen38165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38166" type="x-p"/> 3. Their profound malice appears, farther, in the praises they gave our Lord. Teacher, we know that thou art true, and teachest the way of God. This was indeed the real character of our blessed Lord; and now they bear testimony to the truth, merely with the design to make it subserve their bloody purposes. Those whose hearts are influenced by the spirit of the wicked one never do good, but when they hope to accomplish evil by it. Men who praise you to your face are ever to be suspected. The Italians have a very expressive proverb on this subject: - <div eID="gen38166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38167" type="x-p"/> Che ti fa carezze piu che non suole, O t' ha ingannato, o ingannar ti vuole <div eID="gen38167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38168" type="x-p"/> He who caresses thee more than he was wont to do, has either Deceived thee, or is About To Do It. I have never known the sentiment in this proverb to fail; and it was notoriously exemplified in the present instance. Flatterers, though they speak the truth, ever carry about with them a base or malicious soul. <div eID="gen38168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38169" type="x-p"/> 4. Their malice appears still farther in the question they propose. Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar, or not? - <reference osisRef="Mat.22.17">Mat 22:17</reference>. <div eID="gen38169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38170" type="x-p"/> The constitution of the Jewish republic, the expectations which they had of future glory and excellence, and the diversity of opinions which divided the Jews on this subject, rendered an answer to this question extremely difficult: - <div eID="gen38170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38171" type="x-p"/> 1. In the presence of the people, who professed to have no other king but God, and looked on their independence as an essential point of their religion. <div eID="gen38171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38172" type="x-p"/> 2. In the presence of the Pharisees, who were ready to stir up the people against him, if his decision could be at all construed to be contrary to their prejudices, or to their religious rights. <div eID="gen38172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38173" type="x-p"/> 3. In the presence of the Herodians, who, if the answer should appear to be against Caesar's rights, were ready to inflame their master to avenge, by the death of our Lord, the affront offered to his master the emperor. <div eID="gen38173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38174" type="x-p"/> 4. The answer was difficult, because of the different sentiments of the Jews on this subject; some maintaining that they could not lawfully pay tribute to a heathen governor: while others held that as they were now under this strange government, and had no power to free themselves from it, it was lawful for them to pay what they had not power to refuse. <div eID="gen38174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38175" type="x-p"/> 5.
